|   `c→v` `v→c Favored direction` `ratio` `h` `5.322` `0.064 H → vowel` `83.2` `n` `1.921` `8.025 Vowel → N` `4.18` `w` `1.343` `0.508 W → vowel` `2.64` `b` `1.209` `0.541 B → vowel` `2.23` `s 2.409 4.083 Vowel → S 1.69` `p` `1.391` `0.824 P → vowel` `1.69` `k` `0.338` `0.233 K → vowel` `1.45` `v` `1.308` `0.929 V → vowel` `1.41` `y` `0.288` `0.402 Vowel → Y` `1.4`  |      `f 1.269 1.634 Vowel → F 1.29` `r 4.123 5.258 Vowel → R 1.28` `m` `2.127` `1.661 M → vowel` `1.28` `c` `2.428` `1.978 C → vowel` `1.23` `d` `1.746` `2.118 Vowel → D` `1.21` `g` `0.903` `0.801 G → vowel` `1.13` `t 4.374 3.87 T → vowel 1.13` `l 2.503 2.761 Vowel → L 1.10`  *\* table data: Norvig*  |
| :---- | :---- |

The main takeaway is that **any layout that aims to minimize redirects should place the letter H with the vowels**, as H only combines with them in a single direction (ratio of 83 to 1\!). On the other side of the spectrum, **placing R or T with the vowels will noticeably increase redirects** as they combine with the vowels in both directions about equally.

### 8.8. Common trigrams & redirects 

As a general rule, redirects are the result of increasing rolling in a layout. The following are the main letter patterns that will lead to redirects:

| Rolly (Ec0) `y o u f j  q m w l , i a e n b  k t s r c '  ; " h p z  v d g x .` | Inrolly (Ec0) `y o u q x  k d l w ,   i a e n j  v h t s c '  " - r b z  f p m g .` |
| :---- | :---- |

* **Vowel → consonant → vowel trigrams**. These will inevitably be redirects when all three letters are on the same hand. For example, **ERE**, **ONE** & **ARE** on Inrolly.

* **Consonant → vowel → consonant trigrams**. These would also be redirects if the three letters share one side. For example, **HIN**, **HEN** & **HAN** on Rolly.

* **Vowel → vowel, followed or preceded by a consonant**. These are redirects or 3rolls depending on our vowel setup. For instance, on Inrolly, **EAR** & **AIN** are redirects, but **OUR**, **ION** & **REA** are 3rolls.

* **Consonant only trigrams**. These are redirects or 3rolls depending on our consonant setup. For example, **STR** on Rolly is a redirect.

* **Trigrams with punctuation**. For example, **T'S** is a redirect on either Rolly or Inrolly.

Ideally, we want all three keys in a redirect to share the same row (e.g. **AIN** or **STR** or Rolly). However, in practice many redirects will have just two letters on the same row, while a third letter is on a different row (e.g. **ONE**, **HIN**, **HEN** or **HAN** on Rolly).

Another aspect that affects how a redirect will feel is if it has SFS or not. If it does, then the redirect is typed with just two fingers, as one finger is utilized twice (e.g. **HIN**, **HEN** or **HAN** on Rolly). If there is no SFS, then three fingers will be used (e.g. **AIN**, **ONE** or **STR** on Rolly).

### 8.9. “Weak” redirects

**Redirects where the index finger is not utilized are sometimes referred to as “weak” or “bad” redirects, as they are trickier to type.** Having said that, people who have developed good finger independence and dexterity with their weaker fingers (from playing a musical instrument for example) will probably not mind “weak” redirects at all.

| [Seht Drai](https://github.com/samuelxyz/layouts#seht-drai) (Tanamr) `f u l v b  q g n o j s e h t k  ' d r a i .  ; m p w z  y c x / ,` |  The SHE trigram is a weak redirect on Seht Drai, while STE is not. Similarly, AIN is a weak redirect, but not DON. |  |
| :---- | :---- | ----- |

Most trigrams in the English language (and therefore most redirects) involve both vowels and consonants. Conversely, vowel only trigrams are extremely rare. So, **in order to minimize weak redirects, we must place all the vowels on the same hand and on our last three fingers specifically** (pinky, ring and middle). As such:

| Whix (Ec0) `f l n d k  ' w o u j s r h t v  y c a e i  x b m z q  p g . " ,` |  On the right hand, with consonants being on the index finger, and vowels on middle, ring and pinky, we ensure that any trigram with both vowels \+ consonants will involve the index. |  |
| :---- | :---- | ----- |

It should be noted that, although vowel only trigrams are rare in English, there are actually some common consonant only trigrams. Regardless, with the right letter arrangement we can avoid weak redirects on the consonant hand as well. For example, none of the redirects on Whix’s left hand (**STR**, **NDS**, **RST**, **NST**, **NTS**, **RTH**…) are weak redirects.

### 8.10. Common trigrams & 3rolls

**Layouts that aim to maximize 3rolls necessarily have to split the vowels, placing three vowels on one hand, and two on the other.** This is done so that the most common trigram in the English language (**THE**) can be a 3roll on one hand, while on the other hand we have some of the next most common trigrams as 3rolls too (**ING**, **AND**, **ION**…). An example of such a layout would be Seht Drai (angle modded) which maximizes 3rolls while also doing a great job at optimizing other layout stats like SFBs, SFSs, etc…

| [Seht Drai](https://github.com/samuelxyz/layouts#seht-drai) (Tanamr) `f u l v b  q g n o j s e h t k  ' d r a i .  ; m p w z  y c x / ,` |
| :---- |

The following are the 3rolls on Seht Drai. For each hand, they are sorted based on frequency (on the TypeRacer corpus):

* Left hand: **THE**, **WHE**, **PLE**, **BLE**, **SEL**, **LES**, **TLE**...  
* Right hand: **ING**, **AND**, **ION**, **IND**, **ANY**, **ON'**, **ONG**, **ARD**, **ANG**, **ANC**, **ORD**…

Ideally, we want all the letters in a 3roll to be on the same row (e.g. **THE**, **ONG** or **ARD**). However, we can only have a few 3rolls like that in a layout. The best we can hope for most 3rolls is having two of the letters sharing a row. See all the remaining 3rolls on Seht Drai other than **PLE**, **ANY** and **ANC** (those three have each letter on a different row).

Anyway, **the disadvantage of utilizing a 3-2 vowel split is that alternation plummets**, meaning redirects and long same hand sequences will be way higher than on other layouts.

# Chapter 9: Layout structure (8 min)

### 9.1. Letter stacks

A basic step when making a layout is deciding where the high frequency letters will be. These are **E**, **A**, **O**, **I** for the vowels (which we will highlight in green) and **T**, **N**, **S**, **R**, **H** for the consonants (which will be highlighted in red).

The aforementioned letters are the main ones competing for the 8 home row spots in a layout. **Since there are 9 high frequency letters for 8 home row spots, one of them will inevitably be pushed off the home row.** **The result is that there will always be at least 2 high frequency letters sharing a column/finger. This is referred to as a “stack”.** The viable consonant stacks are **NH, RH** & **NR**, while the vowel stacks are **EO** & **AO**:

| 1 consonant stack: Isrt (Whorf) `y c l m k  z f u , ' i s r t g  p n e a o ; q v w d j  b h / . x` | 1 vowel stack: [Graphite](https://github.com/rdavison/graphite-layout) (StronglyTyped) `b l d w z  ' f o u j ; n r t s g  y h a e i , q x m c v  k p . - /` |  |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |

Despite being less common, **the letter C plays a key role in layouts.** The unique thing about C is that it cannot share a column with T, N, R or H (high SFBs). Therefore, **on 1 stack layouts, C will always be on a SC column** (see the layouts above).

However, there are certain aspects of layout design (SFBs, for example) that can only be fully optimized **if we break the SC pair and give the letter C its own column. And for that, we need 2 stacks** (a consonant stack \+ a vowel stack):

| 2 stacks with C on index: [Sturdy](https://o-x-e-y.github.io/layouts/sturdy/index.html) (Oxey) `v m l c p  x f o u j s t r d y  . n a e i z k q g w  b h ' ; ,` | 2 stacks with C on pinky: Pine (ClemenPine) `y l r m k  q f o u , c s n t g  b h a e i j x z w v  p d ' / .` |
| :---- | :---- |

So, there are 4 main categories: 1 consonant stack, 1 vowel stack, and 2 stacks with either a C index or a C pinky. Layouts in the same category will share more similarities. In the next few pages, we go over the properties shared by layouts in each category.

### 9.2. One consonant stack

Layouts that have two of the top consonants on the same column (e.g. a **NH column**):

| [Colemak DH](https://colemakmods.github.io/mod-dh/) (SteveP) `q w f p b  j l u y ; a r s t g  m n e i o` '  `x c d v z  k h , . /` | [Colemak Qi;x](https://github.com/DreymaR/BigBagKbdTrixPKL/tree/master/Layouts/Colemak/Cmk-Qmods#colemak-qix-by-nyfee-2021-03) (Nyfee) `; l c m k  j f u y q a r s t g  p n e i o '  x w d v z  b h / . ,` | Isrt (Whorf) `y c l m k  z f u , ' i s r t g  p n e a o ;  v w d j q  b h / . x` |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |

**These layouts have the highest home row use, as the letter O** (the 4th most common English letter) **is on the home row.** To make room for O, H is pushed off the home row.

Since one of the main vowels (usually A or I) is moved to the consonant hand, alternation will noticeably decrease. Consequently, rolls, and especially redirects, will increase.

### 9.3. One vowel stack

Layouts that have two of the top vowels on the same column (e.g. an **AO or EO column**):

| [Gallium](https://github.com/GalileoBlues/Gallium) (Brys) `b l d c v  z y o u , n r t s g  p h a e i q x m w j  k f ' ; .` | [Mtgap](https://mathematicalmulticore.wordpress.com/the-keyboard-layout-project/) (Michael Dickens) `y p o u j  k d l c w i n e a ,  m h t s r q z ' . :  b f g v x` | [Rollla](https://github.com/samuelxyz/layouts#rollla) (Tanamr & Heart) `y o u b .  x k c l v i a e n ,  m h s r t  ' / p w z  f d g j q` |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |

**The letter O is now relegated to the top row**, with H taking the home row spot. Therefore, **home row use will be a bit lower**, as H is less frequent than O.

A fundamental difference between the previous subgroup and this one is that **now the vowels take just three home row spots, rather than four.** This allows us to have all vowels on one side, while still being able to fit consonants on that same hand. This way we can have good rolling (from consonants \+ vowels) and low redirects (from one side vowels).

### 9.4. Two stacks (1 vowel \+ 1 consonant)

Layouts that have a vowel stack (**EO or AO**) and a consonant stack (**HN, RN or HR**). **Double stack layouts have the least home row use, but in return they can reach the lowest SFBs.** Most double stack layouts will split S from C. Below we focus on such layouts. Still, it is technically possible to make double stack layouts that retain an SC column.

#### 9.4.1. With C on index

C causes negligible SFBs and SFSs with multiple moderately common letters. We can take advantage of this by placing C on an index finger, to pair it with five other characters:

| [Sturdy](https://o-x-e-y.github.io/layouts/sturdy/index.html) (Oxey) `v m l c p  x f o u j s t r d y  . n a e i  k q g w z  b h ' ; ,` | [Seht Drai](https://github.com/samuelxyz/layouts#seht-drai) (Tanamr) `f u l v b  q g n o j s e h t k  ' d r a i .  ; m p w z  y c x / ,` | [Noctum](https://o-x-e-y.github.io/layouts/noctum/index.html) (Oxey) `b f d l z  j g o u , n s t r k  y c a e i  v m h x q  p w ' ; .` |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |

**The characters C, D, Y, W, G, P, F, B, V and apostrophe can be combined mostly freely as they cause few SFBs among themselves** (one exception is the **BY** SFB). Some C indexes also include the letter M, although M causes SFBs more easily (e.g. **MY**, **MP**, **MB**). Anyway, the table below lists different C index setups and gives a layout example for each:

| With D:  `DC WGP  Semimak`  `DCYWG  Gemini`  `DC WGP   '  Semimak JQ`  `DCY G    '  Seht Drai`  `DC WG  MV  Trance`  `DC W PB  '  Trendy`  `DCYWGP  Sturdy`  | Without D:  `CYWG    F'  Dina`  `C WGPV   '  Rainy`  `CYWGP    '  Whix`  `C WGPV B  Recurva`  `CYWG  M  Stronk`  `C WG VMB  Snug`  `CYWGPV  Whorf`  |  For an easier comparison, letters that appear on multiple rows of the table are kept on the same vertical line. For example, the indexes on Semimak and Gemini share D, C, W & G, but differ on Y & P.  |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |

#### 9.4.2. With C on pinky

One drawback with the layouts in the previous section is that the index finger dedicated to the letter C is a bit underutilized (around 11-14% use). If this is an issue, C can be moved to the pinky instead:

| [Canary](https://github.com/Apsu/Canary#canary) (Eve) `w l y p k  z x o u ; c r s t b  f n e i a '  j v d g q  m h / , .` | Pine (ClemenPine) `y l r m k  q f o u , c s n t g  b h a e i j x z w v  p d ' / .` | [Engram](https://engram.dev/) (Arno Klein) `b y o u '  " l d w v z c i e a ,  . h t s n q g x j k -  ? r m f p` |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |

Compared to C index layouts, **moving C to the pinky sacrifices some SFB and SFS optimization, in favor of more traditional indexes with higher usage.**

The table below lists some C pinky setups. As we go down the table we get into pinky variants with higher movement:

|  `WC  Canary` |
| :---- |
|  **`YC`**  `Pine` |
|  **`WC'`**  `Crest` |
|  **`,C.'`**  `Rolly` |
|  `WCG'  Saiga` |
|  `BCG  Engram` |

### 9.5. Summary table

The table below summarizes the characteristics of the different layout categories. To see the pros and cons of a particular category, go through a row of the table. To compare how the different categories perform on a particular aspect, check a column instead:

|  | Home row use | SFBs | SFSs | Redirects | Index use | Pinky use | Usual vowel hand split |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **1 consonant stack** (NH, RH or NR) | **High** | **Mid** | **Mid** | **High** | **High** | **Mid** | **4 \- 1** |
| **1 vowel stack** (AO or EO) | **Mid** | **Mid** | **Low** | **Variable** | **Low** | **Mid** | **5 \- 0** |
| **2 stacks with C on index** | **Low** | **Low** | **Low** | **Variable** | **Low** | **Mid** | **5 \- 0** |
| **2 stacks with C on pinky** | **Low** | **Mid** | **Low** | **Variable** | **High** | **Low** | **5 \- 0** |

\* It is possible to get “low SFBs” with any of the categories. The reason only the third appears as **Low**, is simply to highlight that it can optimize SFBs further than the others.

\* The word **variable** refers to the redirects being dependent on what consonants are with the vowels. For example, H \+ vowels has low redirects, but NR \+ vowels has high redirects.

We can identify some patterns from the table:

* **Low index finger use correlates with lower SFBs.** Reaching the least SFBs requires using a C index, and those indexes have low use. Having said that, there are layouts that manage to get quite low SFBs while maintaining high index finger use.

* **Low index finger use also correlates with lower SFSs.** The reason for this is straightforward. Since index fingers have six keys assigned to them, there are many more letter interactions on the indexes, all of which can cause SFSs. The purpose of SFS optimization is for each word to be spread across more fingers. Naturally, this means concentrating fewer common letters on any particular finger.

* **Minimal SFSs requires a vowel stack** (an AO column specifically). This is why 1 consonant stack layouts can not reduce SFSs past a certain point. We will elaborate on this in the next chapter.

# Chapter 10: Vowel blocks and punctuation (15 min)

### 10.1. Challenging the home row convention

Old keyboard layouts were designed under the assumption that all the common letters should be kept on the home row. This is perfectly exemplified by Colemak:

| [Colemak](https://colemak.com/) (Shai Coleman) `q w f p g  j l u y ; a r s t d  h n e i o ' z x c v b  k m , . /` |
| :---- |

However, **modern layouts will usually place the letter O** (the fourth most frequent letter in the English language) **outside the home row**, on either an OA or OE column:

| [Graphite](https://github.com/rdavison/graphite-layout) (StronglyTyped) `b l d w z  ' f o u j ; n r t s g  y h a e i , q x m c v  k p . - /` |
| :---- |

Arranging the vowels in a compact way like this is referred to as a vowel block. **The point is to reduce the number of fingers that are dedicated to the vowels** (note how the vowels occupy four fingers on Colemak, but only three on Graphite).

Although this approach will lower home row usage, we get multiple benefits in return:

* Consonants can now be spread across more fingers, ideal for SFB & SFS optimization. This is on top of OA and OE causing low SFBs by themselves.

* We can now have all vowels on one side (which minimizes long same hand sequences and redirects) while still being able to fit consonants on the vowel hand (to increase rolling). So, we get the best of both worlds.

### 10.2. OE stack

**An OE column is a good fit if we do not mind high middle finger usage**, **in order to lower ring finger use**. **The drawbacks are a few SFBs** (the words **people**, **someone** and **does**) **and multiple SFSs** (words like **one**, **more**, **some**, **over**, **those** or **before**). Having said that, these SFS are only 1U and are typed with the strongest finger.

Below we list the common vowel blocks with an OE column. Each vowel block is named after the vowel pairs it utilizes (i.e. which vowels are sharing a column/finger).

#### UA OE YI

| [Mtgap](https://mathematicalmulticore.wordpress.com/the-keyboard-layout-project/) (Michael Dickens) `y p o u j  k d l c w i n e a ,  m h t s r q z ' . :  b f g v x` | The point of this vowel block is to maximize inward rolls (i.e. rolls that go from the outside of the keyboard to the inside). By placing an UA column on the index finger and an OE column on the middle finger, both the OU bigram (on the top row) and the EA bigram (on the home row) become in-rolls. Additionally, having an YI column on ring or pinky makes the IO, IE and IA bigrams inward. The same applies to the word YOU. |  |
| :---- | :---- | ----- |

#### OE UI A

| [Canary](https://github.com/Apsu/Canary#canary) (Eve) `w l y p k  z x o u ; c r s t b  f n e i a '  j v d g q  m h / , .` | With this block we give up inward rotation, as OU and EA become outward. The upside is that having the vowel hand’s consonants on the index finger allows for more comfortable trigrams. For example, compare ION on Mtgap vs Canary. |  |
| :---- | :---- | ----- |

### 10.3. OA stack

**An OA column has lower SFBs and SFSs than EO**. **The one drawback is that ring finger usage will noticeably increase**, as we often get an OA or UE ring.

Despite the letters A and O having similar usage, most of the time it will be A that is on the home row when using an OA column. This is because, since U is already on the top row (UE column) we want O next to U in order to make **OU** a same row roll.

#### OA UE I

| [Graphite](https://github.com/rdavison/graphite-layout) (StronglyTyped) `b l d w z  ' f o u j ; n r t s g  y h a e i , q x m c v  k p . - /` | If the letter Y is on the index finger, the OA column usually goes on the middle finger, and UE on ring. This way YOU is a 3roll. |  |
| :---- | :---- | ----- |

#### UE OA YI

YI on pinky:

| [Semimak JQ](https://semilin.github.io/) (Semi) `f l h v z  ' w u o y s r n t k  c d e a i x j b m q  p g , . /` | Since the letter Y has been moved to the pinky, the OA and UE columns swap fingers when compared to the previous layout. This way YOU remains a 3roll. |  |
| :---- | :---- | ----- |

YI on ring:

| [Uciea](https://www.keyboard-design.com/best-ansi-layouts-conventional.html) (Ian Douglas) `p y u o -  k d h f x q c i e a '  g t n s r v z " , . ;  w m l b j` | Ring finger usage is now lower (YI vs OA/UE). However, YOU becomes a redirect. In this setup, the UE column is not on index, because that would put E with all punctuation (SFBs). |  |
| :---- | :---- | ----- |

#### OA UI E

| [Heart](https://github.com/mindhatch/heart) (\<3) `q c d v k  j y o u ; r s t h l  p n a i e ' w g b m x  z f , . /` | The UE column is replaced with an UI one. This setup is more rare because the letter E (\~12% use) is pushed to the pinky. Layouts that aim to favor in-rolls will swap the OA and UI columns so that the OU bigram becomes an in-roll. |  |
| :---- | :---- | ----- |

### 10.4. Without OE or OA

On layouts without a vowel stack, **the letter O is moved back to the home row, while one of the main vowels** (usually A or I) **is moved to the consonant hand**. Consequently, alternation will decrease, while redirects will increase. On the bright side, home row usage will now be higher, as O is on the home row.

Depending on the location of the A column and the YI one, we have two main variants:

#### UE YI O

| [Colemak Qi;x](https://github.com/DreymaR/BigBagKbdTrixPKL/tree/master/Layouts/Colemak/Cmk-Qmods#colemak-qix-by-nyfee-2021-03) (Nyfee) `; l c m k  j f u y q a r s t g  p n e i o '  x w d v z  b h / . ,` | First we have the colemak approach, where the letter A is the one on the consonant hand. One drawback with this setup is that the common YOU and ION trigrams become redirects. |  |
| :---- | :---- | ----- |

#### UE A O

| Isrt (Whorf) `y c l m k  z f u , ' i s r t g  p n e a o ;  v w d j q  b h / . x` | Alternatively, A and YI can swap places when compared to above. This results in higher rolls and lower redirects (the YOU and ION trigrams are not redirects anymore). The drawback is that the letter Y is now on top row pinky. |  |
| :---- | :---- | ----- |

### 10.5. With an U column (very rare)

It is technically possible to make layouts where the letter U is not sharing a finger with another vowel. Instead, U will be paired with certain consonants. For example, we could use a WUV or a VUK pinky (see Urts). An WUK pinky would be worse because words like **know** or **work** would have K\_W and W\_K 2U skip-2-grams.

| Urts (Ec0) `v l d c f  q b o y ' u r t s w  . n e i a k x m g z  p h ; j ,` |
| :---- |

Although pairing Y with U does not cause SFBs, it creates a Y\_U same finger skip-1-gram on the word **you**. So, the YU pair is only found in layouts that were designed without accounting for SFSs:

| [Hands Down](https://sites.google.com/alanreiser.com/handsdown#h.s6920vg5spfm) (Alan reiser) `q c h p v  k y o j / r s n t g  w u e i a x m l d b  z f ' , .` | Poqtea (Ian Douglas) `y w f l m  k p o q - / u r s n h  d t e a i ' z x c v j  b g , . ;` |
| :---- | :---- |

Regardless, **99 percent of the time the letter U will be in a UE, UA or UI column.**

### 10.6. Avoiding an UIY column

Take a layout with the YI OA UE vowel block:

| Rolly (Ec0) `y o u f j  q m w l , i a e n b  k t s r c '  ; " h p z  v d g x .` |
| :---- |

Now, say E” and YI swapped fingers:

| `" o u f j  q m w l , e a i n b  k t s r c '  ; y h p z  v d g x .` |
| :---- |

From a SFB perspective, both layouts perform about the same. However, typing the common word **you** is much less comfortable on the second layout. This is because of two reasons. Firstly, the **YO** bigram becomes a scissor (an unpleasant bigram where one finger moves upwards and the other downwards). Secondly, **Y\_U** becomes a 2U SFS (our middle finger has to jump over the home row to go from Y to U, with only the letter O in between).

Moving UIY to the ring finger does not fix the problem, as **Y\_U** is still 2U:

| `; u o f j  q m w l , a i e n b  k t s r c '  y " h p z  v d g x .` |
| :---- |

Analyzers that are only optimized for SFBs will often generate layouts with an YIU column. However, the moment we start accounting for SFSs, the analyzer will not suggest an YIU column anymore, as to avoid the **Y\_U** 2U jump.

### 10.7. Punctuation SFBs

We want to identify which are the letters that cause the least SFBs when sharing a finger with each of the three main punctuation symbols (i.e. period, comma and apostrophe).

The corpus utilized to get this data was TypeRacer. The letters are sorted from higher to lower SFBs, and divided by colors into a few groups. The SFBs thresholds are as follows:

**Dark red** \> 0.25%  **Red** \> 0.09%  **Orange** \> 0.05%  **Yellow** \> 0.03%  **Green** \~0.02% or lower

* **SFBs with apostrophe**:

  **T**, **S**, **N**, **I**, **E**, **R**, **U**, **M**, **V**, **L**, **D**, **Y**, **C**, **O**, **A**, **G**, **H**, **W**, **F**, **P**, **B**, **K**

* **SFBs with period**:

  **E**, **S**, **T**, **D**, **N**, **Y**, **R**, **G**, **L**, **M**, **H**, **U**, **O**, **W**, **K**, **P**, **F**, **A**, **C**, **I**, **B**, **V**

* **SFBs with comma** (almost identical to period):

  **E**, **S**, **T**, **Y**, **D**, **N**, **R**, **L**, **G**, **H**, **W**, **O**, **M**, **K**, **U**, **P**, **F**, **A**, **C**, **I**, **B**, **V**

#### 

#### Vowels \+ punctuation

As seen in the SFB data above, **E does poorly with any punctuation. Next, I and U pair well with both period and comma, but not with apostrophe. Lastly, A and O can go with any of the three main punctuation symbols** (although A performs better).

#### Consonants \+ punctuation

**Most common consonants cause SFBs with punctuation. The most relevant exceptions in regard to layouts are the letter H pairing well with apostrophe and C being able to go with any of the three main punctuation symbols.**

#### Other

Period can cause SFB and SFS with a few other keys:

* The end of a paragraph becomes a SFB if period and enter are on the same finger.  
* Capitalizing a letter (period → space → shift) becomes a SFS if period and shift are on the same finger.  
* The end of a quote (.”) becomes a SFB if period and apostrophe share a finger.

### 10.8. Punctuation setup examples

The main factor that determines how punctuation is arranged on a layout is its vowel block.  
**With UA OE YI, all punctuation can go on the UA column** (e.g. see the Heyyou layout below). Alternatively, apostrophe might be moved elsewhere (e.g. Inrolly2, Mtgap). Note that apostrophe being on the OE column (e.g. Mtgap) leads to E → apostrophe becoming a SFB and O\_' being a 2U SFS in contractions like **you’ve** or **you’ll**.

| Heyyou (ClemenPine) `f y o u z  q k l c b h i e a ,  m t r s n j x / . '  g d w v p` | Inrolly2 (Ec0) `p l d w v  ; u o y f n r t s g  . a e i h '  q m c b z  x , " j k` | [Mtgap](https://mathematicalmulticore.wordpress.com/the-keyboard-layout-project/) (Michael Dickens) `y p o u j  k d l c w i n e a ,  m h t s r q z ' . :  b f g v x` |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |

**With OE UI A, either period or comma will go on the UI column and we get an apostrophe \+ A \+ comma/period pinky** (e.g. Canary, Grephati). Some layouts might find another place for apostrophe in order to minimize pinky movement (e.g. Trendei):

| [Canary](https://github.com/Apsu/Canary#canary) (Eve) `w l y p k  z x o u ; c r s t b  f n e i a '  j v d g q  m h / , .` | Grephati (StronglyTyped) `b l d w z  j f o u ' ; n r t s g  y h e i a ,   q x m c v  k p - . /` | Trendei (Ec0) `k l h w '  x f o u q t r n d b  y s e i a  j m c p z  g v - . ,` |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |

**With OA UE I, the basic option is having a comma \+ I \+ period pinky, while apostrophe goes with OA** (e.g. Sntm). If we want lower pinky movement, then apostrophe could go with H (e.g. Graphite) or with C (e.g. Whix) allowing us to move period or comma to OA:

| Sntm (Oxey) `v p d g w  q l o u , s n t m y  x r a e i z b k c f  j h ' ; .` | [Graphite](https://github.com/rdavison/graphite-layout) (StronglyTyped) `b l d w z  ' f o u j ; n r t s g  y h a e i , q x m c v  k p . - /` | Whix (Ec0) `f l n d k  ' w o u j s r h t v  y c a e i  x b m z q  p g . " ,` |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |

**With UE OA YI there is less room for punctuation.** Unlike above, we can no longer place comma and/or period on the I pinky without issues, as that now leads to SFBs with Y. One way to avoid SFBs with this vowel block is utilizing a C \+ punctuation pinky (see Rolly):

| Rolly (Ec0) `y o u f j  q m w l , i a e n b  k t s r c '  ; " h p z  v d g x .` | [Semimak JQ](https://semilin.github.io/) (Semi) `f l h v z  ' w u o y s r n t k  c d e a i x j b m q  p g , . /` | [Recurva](https://github.com/GalileoBlues/Recurva) (Brys) `f r d p v  q j u o y s n t c b  . h e a i z x k g w  m l ; ' ,` |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |

Although this last vowel block generally causes more punctuation SFBs, it is also the vowel block that can reduce SFBs and SFS the most for the letters. Therefore, it will perform better or worse depending on how common punctuation is in our corpora of choice.

### 10.9. Should the index finger be used for consonants or vowels

On layouts that place all the vowels on the same hand, an important decision is whether we want to use the vowel hand's index finger to be used for either consonants or vowels.

#### 10.9.1 Consonant index

| OE UI A | OA UE I |
| :---- | :---- |
| [**Canary**](https://github.com/Apsu/Canary#canary) (Eve) `w l y p k  z x o u ; c r s t b  f n e i a '  j v d g q  m h / , .` | **[Sturdy](https://o-x-e-y.github.io/layouts/sturdy/index.html)** (Oxey) `v m l c p  x f o u j s t r d y  . n a e i  k q g w z  b h ' ; ,` |
| **UE OA YI** | **UI OA E** |
| **[Rollla](https://github.com/samuelxyz/layouts#rollla)** (Tanamr & Heart) `y o u b .  x k c l v i a e n ,  m h s r t  ' / p w z  f d g j q` | **Mir** (RusDoomer) `j o u r q  f d l b g  e a i n x  y h t s c ' / . , z ;  k p m v w` |

The following are reasons in favor of utilizing a consonant index:

* **If we want to increase rolling**, we need to place multiple common consonants on the vowel hand (e.g. NH \+ vowels, HML \+ vowels, NR \+ vowels, etc…). Since we would not want columns like NH on a pinky/ring, they go on the index finger instead.

* Index fingers play a key role on keyboard layouts, as they are assigned six keys each (rather than 3). **If we want to minimize SFBs and SFSs**, it is ideal to reserve both indexes for consonants, as there are many useful six-consonant combinations.

* The simplest way of **minimizing scissors** is to place rare consonants on the bottom row middle, ring and pinky keys (e.g. Canary). Such layouts necessarily use both indexes for consonants. Concentrating more consonants on the indexes also leads to **lower pinky movement**, at the expense of more center column use.

* Compare these two redirects: pinky → index → middle vs pinky → middle → ring. Redirects like the second where the index finger is not utilized are referred to as weak redirects and are usually considered trickier to type.

  So, **if we want to minimize redirects typed with pinky, ring and middle** (i.e. weak redirects) all we have to do is place the vowels on those three fingers. This drastically reduces weak redirects because vowel only trigrams are very rare.

#### 10.9.2 Vowel index

| YI OE UA |  |
| :---- | :---- |
| [**Engram**](https://engram.dev/) (Arno Klein) `b y o u '  " l d w v z c i e a ,  . h t s n q g x j k -  ? r m f p` | **[Mtgap](https://mathematicalmulticore.wordpress.com/the-keyboard-layout-project/)** (Michael Dickens) `y p o u j  k d l c w i n e a ,  m h t s r q z ' . :  b f g v x` |
| **YI UE OA** |  |
| **[Uciea](https://www.keyboard-design.com/best-ansi-layouts-conventional.html)** (Ian Douglas) `p y u o -  k d h f x q c i e a '  g t n s r v z " , . ;  w m l b j` |  |

The following are reasons in favor of utilizing a vowel index:

* **If we want to place the vowels on stronger fingers.** All the vowel blocks in the previous page necessarily placed one vowel on a pinky, and most had either an OA or UE ring (around 15% use). By comparison, the vowel blocks above allow for rings like YI or PN (around 9% usage) by placing vowels on the index finger.  
    
* **If we want to utilize the IY OE UA vowel block**. The point of this vowel setup is to turn **OU** and **EA** into **in-rolls**. In order to do so, a consonant pinky/ring is required, as the middle and index fingers are needed for the OE and UA columns, respectively. The IY OE UA vowel block also helps with **lowering center column use**, but does so at the expense of higher pinky movement.

Although layouts with a vowel index have better hand balance, this is at the expense of most consonants being concentrated on one hand. This results in the consonant having more movement than the vowel hand, particularly in contexts where punctuation is often omitted (e.g. when chatting, word typing tests, etc…).

Another drawback with having most consonants on one hand is that we must be more careful in order to avoid uncomfortable up-down motions (i.e. scissors). Regardless, this can be solved with smart letter placings. For example, Mtgap performs well in this regard, while Uciea does not (compare how the **LF**, **LD** or **LK** bigrams are typed on both layouts).  
10.10. Vowel blocks summary

The table and text explanation below act as a summary for this chapter. Anyway, the main vowel blocks are:

|  Without OA/OE UE YI O (Colemak) UE A O (Isrt)  |  With OA/OE  Consonant index Vowel index OE UI A (Canary) OA UE I (Graphite) UE OA YI (Semimak) OA UI E (Mir) UA OE YI (Mtgap) OA UE YI (Uciea)  |
| :---- | :---- |

Layouts that keep the letter O on the home row (i.e. no OA/OE) have higher home row use, but can not fit all the vowels on the same hand (meaning lower alternation, more redirects).

On layouts with OA/OE, using a consonant index helps with increasing rolling, and lowering SFBs, SFS, scissors, pinky movement and weak redirects. By contrast, a vowel index places the vowels on stronger fingers, plus it helps with lowering center column use and minimizing out-rolls (particularly when combining the UA OE YI block with an H pinky).

As for choosing between OA and OE, vowel blocks with OE have lower ring finger use (e.g. UI, YI) at the expense of higher middle finger usage, SFBs and SFSs. By comparison, OA performs better in those later aspects, but often requires higher use rings (e.g. UE, OA).

# Chapter 11: Consonant blocks (15 min)

### 11.1. Consonant columns table

The table below summarizes the most relevant consonant columns. The table can be useful when making a layout or simply to familiarize ourselves with the common letter patterns (i.e. which letters are often paired together in order to optimize SFBs and SFSs).

If you need help understanding the table, check the table notes in the next page.

|  | Pinky | Ring  | Middle | Index |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **T** | (K|V)T | DT (B|M)TK | DT(K|B|M|G) MT(K|G) or LTM | DTM or DTPB, then some off K, V or G are added. W may be included as well. Sometimes, D goes with H or C instead. |
| **N** | (B|P)N | PNB | HN(B|M|L) RN (may go on ring) LNM | Most N indexes use the NH pair. E.g. FNH(PB|M|PY|BKV) On in-roll layouts, NH is avoided. E.g. NPYF, RNB |
| **S** | (V|F|B)S | FSV or BS(V|F) LS Some of the columns on the middle finger cell. | GS(V|F|W) YS(F|V) CS(V|G|W|F) | S indexes often have 5 of CSGVWYFB. The main potential SFBs when combining those letters are: YS, SC, BY, GS & WS. Ideally, we should avoid having S, C and Y all on the same finger, as that leads to the most SFBs. |
| **H** | FH(K|') | LH | HN(B|M|L) (D|L)HM HRL | With N: FNH(PB|M|PY|BKV) With D: FHDPBKVY can be combined freely as long as BY is avoided. FHDMK also works. With R: LRHK Other: FHPK(Y|BV|YV|Y '), LHM (K|KV) |
| **R** | WR | (W|L)R | LR RN (may go on ring) LR(H|M|W) | R on index is rare as R lacks low SFB pairs. Some index examples are LRHK or RNB. |
| **C** | (W|Y)C WCG ,C.' | Some of the columns on the middle finger cell. | CS(V|G|W|F) | With S (higher use): 5 of CSGVWYFB. The potential SFBs are YS, SC, BY, GS, WS. Without S (lower SFBs): 5/6 of DCYWGPBFMV' Potential SFBs: MY, MP, BY, 'M, MB, DY, 'V. |

The table only lists the letter columns for T, N, S, H, R and C because that already accounts for all the unique consonant columns in keyboard layouts. This is because 99% of the time the remaining consonants will share a column with one of the aforementioned letters. To give an example, the letter D goes with either T, H or C on basically all layouts. So, there is no need to list the columns for D as they are already contained in the rows for T, H and C.

**Table notes:**

To represent letter columns we use the following format: HN(B|M|L). The letters outside the parentheses are locked. Then, we complete the column with one of the options from inside the parentheses. So, in this case we have three options: HNB, HNM and HNL. 

On the columns for the pinky, ring and middle fingers, the first letter given will be the top row character, then the home row, and lastly the bottom row (e.g. HNB has H on the top row). We will use the configuration that leads to the least movement. For instance, for a LRH index the table will show R on the home row, as placing H on the home row instead (i.e. LHR) would noticeably increase movement.

The suggested columns are adapted to that finger’s strength. For example, a high movement column like HNL can go on a middle finger, but not on a ring or pinky. Columns with low movement and no SFBs (e.g. VSX, WCQ) are a good fit for the pinky. Finally, columns for the ring finger would be somewhere in between (e.g. LRJ, PNB).

To help with readability, the letters X, J, Q and Z are omitted from the table. So, for example, when the table only specifies two letters (e.g. a WR pinky) in a place where we are supposed to have three letters, it is because we must complete the column with X, J, Q or Z (e.g. WRX). The same applies to, for example, a FNHPB index. That is five letters. So, we would complete that index column with one rare character.

### 11.2. Consonant blocks table

The table in the previous section can look intimidating to someone that is just getting started with keyboard layouts. Thankfully, there are certain recurring consonant patterns that, once we are aware of, will make it much easier to construct layouts. We will refer to these patterns as consonant blocks. They will be, along with vowel blocks, the foundation around which to build a layout.

**Consonant blocks can be divided into four main groups: with a NH stack, a RH one, a RN one, or with no consonant stack at all.** On the table below, each of the aforementioned groups corresponds to a row on the table. Inside a given group, the different consonant blocks are subdivided depending on where the letter L is located (see the columns on the table below). So, for example, layouts with a NH stack may be split into ones that use a HNL column or layouts that use LR instead. Anyway, for each consonant block a layout example is given in parenthesis:

|  | LH | LR  | LN | LS | LT |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| HN | WR \+ HNL (Colemak) | LR \+ HNB (Sturdy) LR \+ HNM (Canary) | WR \+ HNL (Colemak) |  |  |
| HR | FSV \+ LRH (Noctum) PNB \+ LRH (Sntm) | FSV \+ LRH (Noctum) PNB \+ LRH (Sntm) |  |  |  |
| RN | LH \+ RN (Whix2) RN \+ LHM (Recurva) |  |  | LS \+ RN (Pine) | LT \+ RN (Mir) |
| No HN/HR/RN | LHM \+ CS (Snorkle) | LR \+ CS (Graphite) | LN \+ CS (APT) LNM \+ CS (Hands Down Neu) |  | LT \+ CS (Mtgap) |

As already seen in chapter 10, most layouts nowadays use vowel blocks that compact the vowels on just three fingers. This when combined with a HN/HR/RN stack (the first three rows on the table) gives us room to split S from C. On layouts without HN/HR/RN (last row on the table) we do not have that additional room, so a SC column is required instead.

On the above table, some cells were left blank. This is simply because those options are hardly utilized in layouts:

* LN \+ HR or LS \+ HN/HR are made redundant by LR \+ NH as they do not allow for anything unique over the latter while resulting in worse stats. On the layout examples below, there is no much reason to use anything other than LR \+ HN:

| LR \+ HN | LN \+ HR | LS \+ HN | LS \+ HR |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| `v l h k q  j w o i ' s r n t p  y c e u a z x m d b  f g ; . ,` | `v h l k q  j w o i ' s r n t p  y c e u a z x m d b  f g ; . ,`  | `w l h v q  j p o i ' r s n t b  y c e u a z x m d k  f g ; . ,` | `b l h k q  j w o i ' n s r t p  y c e u a z x m d v  f g ; . ,` |

* LR/N \+ RN were left in black because it involves a RNL column. Most layouts will avoid that option as it leads to high movement (some 2U SFBs and SFSs).

* Without HN/HR/RN, LS is not used because S is reserved for the letter C instead.

* Finally, the LT pair is rarely utilized in layouts because it introduces the LT and TL SFBs (normally, T is one of the letters that cause the least SFBs in layouts). Regardless, LT is necessary in some inward rotation layouts (Mir, Mtgap,…). When looking for in-rolls, NH is counterproductive. Therefore, LT \+ NH is not used. HR is only seen in the form of a LHR column. So, LT \+ HR is not used either.

### 11.3. Combining vowel and consonant blocks

By using the vowel blocks seen in chapter 10 and the consonants blocks seen earlier, we can construct layouts more easily. Here is an example of how to build a layout in steps:

1. **Choose a vowel block** (summarized on section 10.10). This will also determine how punctuation is placed. Say we choose OA UE I:

| `* * * * *  * * o u , * * * * *  * * a e i * * * * *  * * ' ; .` |
| :---- |

2. **Decide which of the main consonants we want on the vowel hand**. As explained in sections 8.4 and 8.5, this will determine whether the layout favors alternation or rolling. Imagine we pick H (which gives high alternation, yet solid rolling):

| `* * * * *  * * o u , * * * * *  * h a e i * * * * *  * * ' ; .` |
| :---- |

3. **Select a consonant pinky.** Starting by the pinky will make it easier to later select a consonant block. Our main pinky options are N, S, H, R, C and T. Each has its pros and cons. Suppose we do not like repeats (e.g. SS) on the pinky and decide on N:

| `* * * * *  * * o u , n * * * *  * h a e i * * * * *  * * ' ; .` |
| :---- |

4. **Choose a consonant block** (section 11.2) **and complete the home row**. With N on the pinky we can discard all the consonant blocks that use a NH or RN stack, as we would not want such columns on a pinky. Our remaining options are using either a HR stack, or not using any consonant stack (i.e. no NH/RN/HR). Imagine we go with the later option and use the LR \+ CS block. Most of the time, the LR column goes on the ring finger. That leaves the middle and index fingers for the letters T and S:

| `* l * c *  * * o u , n r t s *  * h a e i * * * * *  * * ' ; .` |
| :---- |

5. **Finalize the remaining columns** with the help of the consonant column table (section 11.1). For our layout example, we would check the cells for the N pinkies, T middles, and the S and H index variations. The Gallium layouts is a possible result:

| `b l d c v  j f o u ,  n r t s g  y h a e i x q m w z  k p ' ; .` |
| :---- |

Below we build three additional layout examples using the aforementioned steps:

1. Choose a vowel block. We use first UA OE YI, then UE OA YI and lastly OA UE I:

| `* * * * *  * u o * y * * * * *  , a e * i * * * * *  * . ' * *` | `* * * * *  * * u o y * * * * *  * * e a i * * * * *  * * , . *` | `* * * * *  * * o u , * * * * *  * * a e i * * * * *  * * ' / .` |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |

2. Decide which of the main consonants we want on the vowel hand. For the first layout we use the letter N, for the second D and for the third H:

| `* * * * *  * u o * y * * * * *  , a e n i * * * * *  * . ' * *` | `* * * * *  * * u o y * * * * *  * d e a i * * * * *  * * , . *` | `* * * * *  * * o u , * * * * *  * h a e i * * * * *  * * ' / .` |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |

3. Select a consonant pinky. We use R for the first, then S and finally C:

| `* * * * *  * u o * y r * * * *  , a e n i * * * * *  * . ' * *` | `* * * * *  * * u o y s * * * *  * d e a i * * * * *  * * , . *` | `* * * * *  * * o u , c * * * *  * h a e i * * * * *  * * ' / .` |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |

4. Choose a consonant block and complete the home row. For the first layout we use the CS \+ LT block, for the second LR \+ HNB and for the third LS \+ RN:

| `* c l * *  * u o * y r s t h *  , a e n i * * * * *  * . ' * *` | `* l h * *  * * u o y s r n t *  * d e a i * * b * *  * * , . *` | `* l r * *  * * o u , c s n t *  * h a e i * * * * *  * * ' / .` |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |

5. Finalize the remaining columns with the help of the consonant column table (section 11.1). Below are some possible solutions. The first layout is Mtgap (mirrored), the second Semimak JQ and the third Pine:

| `w c l d k  j u o p y r s t h m  , a e n i x v g f b  ; . ' z q` | `f l h v z  ' w u o y   s r n t k  c d e a i x j b m q  p g , . /`  | `y l r m k  q f o u , c s n t w  p h a e i j x z g v  b d ' / .` |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |

### 11.4. Bottom row use on the consonant side

On many layouts the vowel hand’s bottom row middle, ring and pinky keys have low usage as they are utilized for punctuation or rare letters. Consequently, there is a low amount of up-down motion on the vowel side. By comparison, consonant hands are more varied.

Some layouts will minimize the usage of the bottom row non index keys on the consonant hand as well. Doing this results in both hands being closer in feel. Moreover, there will be virtually no scissors. Examples of consonant setups that we can use for this purpose are LS/LH \+ RN (see Pine or Whix2 below), DT \+ LR (see Stronk) among others. Note how the highlighted keys are reserved for rare letters only:

| Pine (ClemenPine) `y l r m k  q f o u , c s n t g  b h a e i j x z w v  p d ' / .` | Whix2 (Ec0) `b l n d k  ' f o u j s h r t w  y c a e i z q x m v  p g . " ,` | [Stronk](https://o-x-e-y.github.io/layouts/stronk/index.html) (Oxey) `f d l b v  j g o u , s t r n k  y m a e i z q x h p  w c ' ; .` |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |

Although the approach above is great at minimizing up-down motions, it has the drawback that more letters are pushed to the indexes. Consequently, index finger load and center column use will increase. If we want to avoid that, then we must place more common letters on the consonant bottom row. Examples of layouts that do that are layouts with the YI OE UA vowel block (see Heyyou) or layouts with a LRH column (see Noctum or Sntm):

| Heyyou (ClemenPine) `f y o u z  q k l c b h i e a ,  m t r s n j x / . '  g d w v p` | [Noctum](https://o-x-e-y.github.io/layouts/noctum/index.html) (Oxey) `b f d l z  j g o u , n s t r k  y c a e i q v m h x  p w ' ; .` | Sntm (Oxey) `v p d g w  q l o u , s n t m y  x r a e i z b k c f  j h ' ; .` |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |

Layouts that use this second approach have a higher potential for scissors. Regardless, it is still possible to keep the scissors low with smart letter placings, which the layouts above do. 

In the remainder of this chapter we analyze the different consonant blocks in more detail.

### 11.5. HN stack

Excluding rare letters, the letters that cause the least SFBs when added to an HN column are, in order: B, M, F, L and P. Having said that, some of these letters cannot share a column among themselves. For instance, P and B should not share a column with L (PL & BL SFBs), or with M (MP & MB SFBs), and F should not go with L (LF & FL SFBs).

The most popular option to avoid the aforementioned SFBs is using **a FNHPB index** or similar and pair it with a **LR ring or middle** (see the Rolly and Sturdy layouts below). An alternative is a **FNHM index** (see Canary). Rather than on index, NH may also go on a **HNB middle** (see Semimak) or a **HNM middle** (see Dhorf and Trendy).

#### LR \+ HNB

| [Semimak JQ](https://semilin.github.io/) (Semi) `f l h v z  ' w u o y s r n t k  c d e a i x j b m q  p g , . /` | [Sturdy](https://o-x-e-y.github.io/layouts/sturdy/index.html) (Oxey) `v m l c p  x f o u j s t r d y  . n a e i  k q g w z  b h ' ; ,` | Rolly (Ec0) `y o u f j  q m w l , i a e n b  k t s r c '  ; " h p z  v d g x .` |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |

#### LR \+ HNM

| [Canary](https://github.com/Apsu/Canary#canary) (Eve) `w l y p k  z x o u ; c r s t b  f n e i a '  j v d g q  m h / , .` | [Dhorf](https://o-x-e-y.github.io/layouts/dhorf/index.html) (Oxey) `v l h k q  j f o u , s r n t w  y c a e i  x m d b z  p g ' ; .` | Trendy (StronglyTyped) `k l h w '  x f o u q t r n d b  y s a e i  j m c p z  g v . - ,` |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |

Each of these setups have their pros and cons. For instance, HNB has by far the least SFSs. Still, some may prefer using a HNM column instead, as concentrating more movement on a strong finger makes it easier to place less movement elsewhere (e.g. on a pinky). One drawback with HNB is that if LR and HNB are on adjacent fingers, then the common BL bigram becomes a scissor (see Semimak). The LR \+ HNM pairing (see Dhorf) avoids that issue entirely, as the scissor now becomes ML, which is a much more rare bigram. An LR \+ YSV setup (see Canary) also causes minimal scissors, as LV is rare. Similarly, LR \+ WSG (see Rolly) performs solidly at scissors, as GL is not very common.

#### WR \+ HNL

| [Colemak DH](https://colemakmods.github.io/mod-dh/) (SteveP) `q w f p b  j l u y ; a r s t g  m n e i o` '  `x c d v z  k h , . /` | [Uciea pcrw](https://www.keyboard-design.com/best-ansi-layouts-conventional.html) (Philipp Kiefer) `p y u o -  k m h b x q c i e a ,  d t n s r w z j ' . ;  f g l v /` |  |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |

An **HNL column** is also possible. We should be careful when utilizing this option as it can easily lead to high movement when placed on an index (see the LNHMK index on colemak). HNL can also lead to scissors (see the ,L bigram on Colemak, or BL and LK on Uciea pcrw).

### 11.6. HR stack

The only good option with a HR stack is a **HRL column.** In such a setup, the letter R should go on the home row (otherwise the RL SFB in words like world becomes 2U). The LRH column can go on either the index or the middle finger. Here is how they compare:

| [Noctum](https://o-x-e-y.github.io/layouts/noctum/index.html) (Oxey) `b f d l z  j g o u , n s t r k  y c a e i  v m h x q  p w ' ; .` | With LRH on the left index, the LR SFB becomes a comfortable alt finger on standard keyboards (R with index, L with middle). Same applies to the RK and LK SFBs (R/L with middle, K with index). Additionally, the very common TH bigram becomes an inward roll. Finally, the common STR trigram is a 3roll. |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Flow** (Ec0) `v p h m z  j f o u ' s n r t x  y c e i a  b l d k q  g w " . ,` | With a HRL middle, we remove the RK and LK SFBs. However, the LR SFB is not a comfortable alt finger anymore, TH is now an out-roll, and STR becomes a redirect. Lastly, L being on the bottom row middle finger key will often lead to more scissors. |

Because of the above reasons, **LRH on index is generally seen as a better option**. Regardless, LRH can be paired with a **FSV or PNB column**. Of these two, PNB is less versatile because it causes scissors more easily. For example, if PNB is adjacent to a DTM column, then either the MP or the MB bigrams become scissors (see the Santa layout below). However, if the pairing is FSV \+ DTM (see Noctum) then there is no issue, as neither F or V combine with the letter M. Technically, in Noctum's case the scissor would now be MB, but that is less problematic because it does not involve adjacent fingers. PNB also performs worse when placed next to the letter L, as either PL or BL become scissors (see Flow). In any case, these issues can be avoided with strategic letter placings. For example, a PNB column does not cause scissors when paired with a DTK column (see Sntm) .

#### FSV \+ LRH

| [Noctum](https://o-x-e-y.github.io/layouts/noctum/index.html) (Oxey) `b f d l z  j g o u , n s t r k  y c a e i  v m h x q  p w ' ; .` | Nstd (Oxey) `b f m g p  z l o u , n s t d y  j r a e i q v k c w  x h ' ; .` | [Engram](https://engram.dev/) (Arno Klein) `b y o u '  " l d w v z c i e a ,  . h t s n q g x j k -  ? r m f p` |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |

#### PNB \+ LRH

| Santa (Oxey) `v p d l j  q w o u , s n t r k  y c a e i  b m h x z  g f ' ; .` | Sntm (Oxey) `v p d g w  q l o u , s n t m y  x r a e i z b k c f  j h ' ; .` | Flow (Ec0) `v p h m z  j f o u ' s n r t x  y c e i a  b l d k q  g w " . ,` |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |

### 11.7. RN stack

When utilizing a HN or HR stack we are limited on what letters we can pair with H. For example, the letter D causes no SFBs with H, but it does with N and R. Therefore, if H is on a HN or HR column, we can no longer use the HD pair.

To take full advantage of H’s pairing we must decouple H from R/N. To do that, we can pair N and R together, on a RN stack, away from H. **Often, the RN column is completed with rare letters** (i.e. X, J, Q, Z) in order to avoid 2U SFBs and SFSs with R. Some of the columns that become possible when using a RN stack are **a LHM middle or index** (see Seht Drai, Recurva), **a LH ring** (see Whix2) **or H indexes with D, Y or K** (see Pine, Kuntum, Saiga…).

#### LHM or LH \+ RN

| [Seht Drai](https://github.com/samuelxyz/layouts#seht-drai) (Tanamr) `f u l v b  q g n o j s e h t k  ' d r a i .  ; m p w z  y c x / ,` | [Recurva](https://github.com/GalileoBlues/Recurva) (Brys) `f r d p v  q j u o y s n t c b  . h e a i z x k g w  m l ; ' ,` | Whix2 (Ec0) `b l n d k  ' f o u j s h r t w  y c a e i  q x m v z  p g . " ,` |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |

#### LS \+ RN

| Pine (ClemenPine) `y l r m k  q f o u , c s n t g  b h a e i j x z w v  p d ' / .` | Kuntum (Lela) `v l n d k  j w o u , t s r h f  g c a e i  z x p b '  m y q / .` | Putih (Lela) `m l r p k  q y o u , h s n t v  f c a e i  z x d b j  g w ' / .` |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |

#### LT \+ RN

| Saiga (RusDoomer) `. o u r q  f d l b w   i a e n x  y h t s c ' , ; / j z  k p m v g` | Inrolly (Ec0) `y o u q x  k d l w ,   i a e n j  v h t s c '  " - r b z  f p m g .` | Gust (Oxey) `; u o f j  q k l r v e i a c y  d h t n s  , . p g '  b m w x z` |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |

Some of these consonant blocks are great at avoiding scissors, as they only place rare letters on the bottom row (see LS \+ RN on Pine, or LH \+ RN on Whix2). Setups that place more common letters on the bottom row may introduce a few scissors (e.g. RK on Recurva, MB on Saiga). One drawback with the RN stack is that it usually leads to a higher load on the ring finger (e.g. rings like LS or RN). By comparison, HRL leads to lighter rings (FSV or PNB) at the expense of higher bottom row use and some potential scissors. So, everything has its tradeoffs. Finally, the LT pair seen above is not used in most layouts, as it causes significant SFBs. For the most part, LT is a concession only made in some in-roll layouts.

### 11.8. Without HN, HR or RN

A side effect of not using any of three consonant stacks is that the letter C will necessarily be on the S column. This is different from most of the layouts in the previous pages. **The CS column is usually completed with one or more of: V, W, G or F**.

On layouts without a consonant stack, similarly to layouts with a RN stack, we have a lot of freedom to put different letters on the H column without that leading to significant SFBs.

#### LR \+ CS

# Chapter 12: Layouts with thumb keys (6 min)

### 12.1. Benefits of placing a letter on the thumb

Most keyboard layouts are designed for standard keyboards (i.e. a laptop) as that is what most people use. One shortcoming with standard keyboards is that only one thumb is utilized (the space bar one). [Ergonomic keyboards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ergonomic_keyboard) often address this by introducing additional thumb keys, allowing us to place a letter on the non-space thumb.

**By having a thumb letter we gain another home row spot.** For example, below we have two versions of the same layout. One without a thumb key and one with R on thumb. We can see that the letter H is pushed off the home row on the former, but not on the later:

| `b f h m q  ' w o u j n s r t k  y c a e i x v l d z  p g . ; ,` | `b f l m q  ' w o u / n s h t k  y c a e i x v j d z  p g . ; ,       r` |
| :---- | :---- |

**Thumb keys will also reduce the amount of SFBs and SFSs in the layout.** For instance, the thumb layout above has a LH middle finger, which is a great improvement when compared to HRL on the non thumb version (HRL introduces the **HR** and **LR** SFBs, the **H\_R** and **L\_R** SFSs, plus it also makes **H\_L** 2U). Furthermore, layouts with a letter on thumb have an easier time avoiding scissors (e.g. **LF** and **BL** are scissors on the non thumb version).

Thumb keys are particularly useful for layouts with a vowel index. The main drawback with such layouts is that they concentrate too many letters on the consonant hand. This can be partly mitigated with a thumb key, as now those letters will be spread across five fingers. For example, below we have two layouts with the UA OE YI vowel block. One with a thumb key and one without. Note how the pinky load is much lower on the thumb version (WC pinky vs BNP pinky). Additionally, the version with R on thumb has noticeably lower SFSs:

| `b c l k q  z u o y f n s r t m  , a e i h p v w d g  ' . ; x j` | `w f l k j  z u o y b c s n t v  , a e i h q g m d p  ' . ; x /       r` |
| :---- | :---- |

To sum up, on standard keyboards it is only possible to optimize layouts up to a certain point. Placing a letter on thumb allows us to optimize layouts a bit further.

### 12.2. On what hand should the thumb letter be?

**If the thumb letter is a vowel, it will often go on the vowel hand. If the layout uses a consonant thumb instead, it will be moved to the consonant side.** The idea behind this is to keep the vowels together, to prevent low alternation and high redirects. For example, below we have a standard layout and two mods of it that use a thumb letter:

| `Sturdy (Oxey) v m l c p  x f o u j s t r d y  . n a e i z k q g w  b h ' ; ,` | `SturdE (Oxey) v m l c p  ; x o , / s t r d y  f n a i u q k j w g  b h ' . z                e`   | `Strand (Valorance) v m l f q  ' y o u . s t r h b  g c a e i z j x d k  p w ; / ,       n`  |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |

We can see that the thumb letter changes hands depending if it is a vowel or a consonant. Regardless, each of the mods above has its pros and cons. SturdE has high rolling and a lower load on the ring and pinky fingers. By comparison, Strand has higher alternation, lower SFSs and lower thumb repeats.

### 12.3. Which should be the thumb letter?

The first letter that people placed on the thumb was E. Intuitively, it makes sense to place the most frequent letter in the English language on a strong finger like the thumb. For example, that is what the Maltron layout did in 1977:

| `Maltron (Lilian Malt) q p y c b  v m u z l a n i s f  d t h o r , . j g ;  / w k - x       e` |
| :---- |

An important consideration is that quickly double tapping a key is trickier with the thumb than with the other fingers. Consequently, **one may want to avoid having the most common double letters on the thumb.** Among the top letters, the repeats are:

| `LL` | `SS` | `EE` | `OO` | `TT` | `RR` | `NN` | `II` | `AA` | `HH` |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| `0.58` | `0.41` | `0.38` | `0.21` | `0.17` | `0.12` | `0.07` | `0.02` | `0.00` | `0.00` |

Another aspect we can look into is the ability of each letter to be paired with others without causing SFBs. Of the top consonants, the letter H performs best in that regard, followed by T, N, S and lastly R. Letters with lots of low SFB pairs (e.g. H, T) are better exploited on the indexes, where they can be paired with five other letters. By contrast, **letters with poor pairs (e.g. R) fit perfectly on the thumb, as they will be alone there and will not cause SFBs and SFSs**. One could argue that letters with great pairings are wasted on the thumb.

### 12.4. Consonants on the thumb

If one is satisfied with the vowel blocks shown in [chapter 10]() then we can leave the vowels unchanged and dedicate the thumb to a consonant. **Most layouts with a consonant thumb will have an OA or OE stack but will no longer need an HN, HR or RN stack.**

**On modern layouts R has become the most popular thumb key**. Below we have some examples. They are split into two groups, depending if they use a consonant or vowel index on the vowel hand. The pros and cons of each approach were explained on section 10.9.

With a consonant index:

| `Dusk x f d p q  j ' o u . n s t c y  m h a e i b v k g w  z l _ / ,       r` | `Night (Valorance) b f l k q  p g o u . n s h t m  y c a e i x v j d z  ' w ; / ,       r` | `Snth (Phbonachi) x p d m q  = y o u , s n t h v  g c a e i f b k l j  z w ' / .       r` |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |

With a vowel index:

| `Hands Down Titanium j g m p v  # . / " ' c s n t k  , a e i h  x f l d w  - u o y b        r` | `Hands Down Rhodium ' b h g "  # . / j x c s n t k  , a e i m p f l d v  - u o y w       r` | `Hands Down Promethium f p d l x  ; u o y b z s n t h k  , a e i c q v w g m j  - . ' = /       r` |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **`Enthium`** `(Sunaku)   b y o u ;  x l d w v z c i e a ,  k h t n s q   ' - = . /  j m g p f                r` | **`Eahi`** `(Valorance) b f m c p  q u o l . n s t d y  z e a h i x v k w g  / ; ' j ,       r` |  |

It is also perfectly viable to place letters other than R on the thumb.

With a consonant index:

| `Really (Valorance) b f d g p  q j u o . n s t c y  m r e a i x v k w '  z l / ; ,       h` | `Day (dalaning) b f l k q  p g o u , n s r t m  y c a e i x v j d z  ' w ; / .       h` | `Sunrise (dalaning) b f l p w  ' m o u , n s r c y  k h a e i x v j g q  z d ; / .       t` |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **`Strand`** `(Valorance) v m l f q  ' y o u . s t r h b  g c a e i z j x d k  p w ; / ,       n` | **`Morning`** `(dalaning) j f l d q  p g o u , r s h t k  y c a e i x v m b z  ; w ' / .       n` | **`Afternoon`** `(dalaning) f l d v z  p g o u , s r h t k  y c a e i x j b m q  ' w ; / .       n`                |
| **`Bunya`** `(Brys) b l m c z  j f o u , n r t d p  y h a e i x q v g w  ; k ' / .        s` | **`North`** `(Valorance) b l m d z  q w o u , n r t h f  c y a e i x j v p k  ' g ; / .       s`             |  |

With a vowel index:

| [`Hands Down Bronze`](https://sites.google.com/alanreiser.com/handsdown/home/hands-down-neu#h.e0hh8lan9rtv) `j g m p v  ; . / ' " r s n t b  , a e c i x f l d k  - u o w y       h` | [`Hands Down Gold`](https://sites.google.com/alanreiser.com/handsdown/home/hands-down-neu#h.8i2msuo3butx) `j g m p v  ; . / " ' r s n d b  , a e i h  x f l c w  - u o y k        t` | `Hands Down Silver j f m p v  ; . / ' " r s h t b  , a e c i x g l d k  - u o u y       n` |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |

### 12.5. Vowels on the thumb

All the layouts in the previous section used an **OE** or **OA** stack. **If we want to move the letter O back to the home row, then we would place a vowel on the thumb.** Below we have some examples of vowel blocks with a vowel thumb:

| E on thumb | A on thumb |
| :---- | :---- |
| `* * * * * * * u . ' * * * * * * * i a o * * * * * * * , ; /                e`   | `* * * * * * * u . ' * * * * * * * e i o * * * * * * * ; , /                a`   |
| **I on thumb** | **O on thumb** |
| `* * * * * * * u . ' * * * * * * * e o a * * * * * * * ; , /                i`  | `* * * * * * * u . ' * * * * * * * e i a * * * * * * * ; , /                o` |

The letter E makes the most use of the thumb, but it also causes the most repeats, followed by O. By contrast, A or I do not have repeats.

Some layouts may still have an OA or OE column even if they have a vowel on thumb:

| `SturdE (Oxey) v m l c p  ; x o , / s t r d y  f n a i u q k j w g  b h ' . z                e`   | `Rusty (dalaning) q b d w g  j l o u ' r s t y p  m n a i h x v k c f  z / . , ;                e` |  |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |

# Chapter 13: Layout subgroups (8 min)

### 13.1. Classifying layouts

Because of the sheer number of layouts, it is very difficult to decide which layout to learn when looking at layouts as a whole. To help us with this issue, **we will separate layouts into five main categories**:

* **Colemak-like**: Self explanatory.  
* **In-roll**: Layouts that favor rolls going toward the center of the keyboard.  
* **High roll-mid redirect**: Layouts that increase rolling without sacrificing redirects.  
* **3 roll**: Layouts that not only want to increase 2rolls, but 3rolls as well.  
* **Alternation**: Layouts that favor alternation over rolling.

**Inside a given category, layouts will be further subdivided according to which consonants they place on the vowel hand.** For example, high roll \- mid redirect layouts can be split into two main subgroups: NH \+ vowels and HML \+ vowels. 

**These subcategories can then be split again based on the home row on the consonant side.** For instance, the aforementioned NH \+ vowels subgroup has four main home rows to choose from: CRST, STRD, SRTD and SRTC.

**Finally, we can also classify the home rows based on which letter columns they use.** For instance, the CRST home row leads to double stack layouts (i.e. OE/OA column \+ NH column) with a C pinky, while STRD, SRTD and SRTC lead to layouts with a C index instead.

Later in this document, each of the five main categories will get their own chapter. There we will establish how to construct each layout type and highlight its benefits. Additionally, we will also be listing plenty of layout examples for each category, including their stats.

### 13.2. Layout stat table

When comparing layouts, we will first show each layout in a text format. The top consonants will be highlighted in red and the vowels in green. The letter C will also be highlighted (in black) because of its importance in layout structure. Here is an example:

| [Noctum](https://o-x-e-y.github.io/layouts/noctum/index.html) (Oxey) `b f d l z  j g o u , n s t r k  y c a e i  v m h x q  p w ' ; .` | [Mtgap](https://mathematicalmulticore.wordpress.com/the-keyboard-layout-project/) (Michael Dickens) `y p o u j  k d l c w i n e a ,  m h t s r q z ' . :  b f g v x` | Isrt (Whorf) `y c l m k  z f u , ' i s r t g  p n e a o ;  v w d j q  b h / . x` |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |

Afterward, the stats will be compiled on a table, as such:

|  | SFB | SFS | Scissors | Alt | Roll | Redir | In:out-roll | Pinky off | Hand use |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Noctum** | **Very low** 0.550 | **Very low** 5.556 | **Mid low** 0.26 | **High** 41.1 | **Mid low** 43.3 | **Low** 4.1 | **Low** 1.5 | **Mid** 4.5 | **Even** 48 – 52 |
| **Mtgap** | **Mid** 1.048 | **Mid** 6.661 | **Low** 0.23 | **Mid high** 37.2 | **Mid** 45 | **Mid low** 5 | **Mid low** 2 | **Mid** 5.1 | **Even** 51 – 49 |
| **Isrt** | **Very low** 0.599 | **Mid low** 6.484 | **Very low** 0.12 | **Mid low** 31.4 | **Very high** 49.6 | **High** 8.9 | **Min** 0.8 | **Low** 3.5 | **Even** 48 – 52 |

You should already be familiar with most of these stats. The “**in:out-roll**” stat is the result of dividing the number of in-rolls and out-rolls in a layout. In other words, it tells how much a layout favors inward rotation. The “**pinky off**” stat tells us how often our pinky has to move off the home row and press a key on the top or bottom row.

**If a layout performs great in one stat, then that stat will appear in green. If the layout performs decently, then we will use yellow. If it performs poorly, then red**. Most stats are shown in green when they are low (SFB, SFS, Scissors, Redir and Pinky off). However, alternation, rolls and in:out-roll will be shown in green when they are high. Lastly, hand usage gets worse the furthest away it is from even.

Note that a layout having more stats in green does not necessarily make it better than another. That would only be true if all the stats were of the same importance. On the contrary, **how each stat is valued will vary from person to person**. For example, if someone likes high alternation, they will likely discard any layout that fails to optimize said stat. Meanwhile, others might focus on the rolling or pinky off stats instead. Some people prefer layouts with a high in:out-roll ratio, while others disregard that stat entirely. In any case, the minimum requirement for a layout is that it performs decently at SFBs and SFSs.

### 13.3. How the stats were obtained

**The SFB, SFS, alt, roll and redir stats were taken from the [Genkey](https://semilin.github.io/genkey/) analyzer**. Since Genkey does not give the remaining stats, those were obtained elsewhere. **The scissor stat comes from [keysolve](https://grassfedreeve.github.io/keysolve-web/). The in:out roll** (i.e. in-roll ratio) **and hand use stats are from [a200](https://github.com/Apsu/200-analyzer)**. For the pinky off stat a simple tool was used to check the frequency of the characters that each layout places on the top and bottom row pinky positions.

**The corpus used with all the analyzers was [MonkeyRacer](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1w7abBPxVGQAY1b0dG9bNBEmXwAEkcQyo/view?usp=drive_link)** (a combination of the quotes on [MonkeyType](https://monkeytype.com/) and [TypeRacer](https://play.typeracer.com/), but removing the duplicates). The reason for utilizing this corpus is that MonkeyType and TyperRacer are popular typing websites. A peculiarity of the MonkeyRacer corpus is that punctuation (period, comma and apostrophe) play a bigger role than in other corpora. Additionally, since the most frequent English words are also heavily represented in the corpus, letters like W and Y become more common.

### 13.4. Stats thresholds

For full transparency, in this section we list the ranges that were utilized in order to place each stat in the “**low**”, “**mid**” or “**high**” categories.

**Stats that one may want to maximize** (i.e. alternation, rolling and in:out-roll) **can be referred to as positive. For these, the full range for each stat was used.** This means that we checked what was the lowest and highest point for a given stat, and then evenly split the “**Min**” to “**Max**” categories across that range. It should be noted that the most extreme values require ruining key stats like SFBs, so those values were excluded.

In the table below, each cell indicates the highest value for a given category. For instance, 38.3 alternation qualifies as “**Mid high**”, but anything past that counts as “**High**” (until 41.2).

|  | Min | Very low | Low | Mid low | Mid | Mid high | High | Very high | Max |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Alt** | 23.9 | 26.8 | 29.7 | 32.6 | 35.4 | 38.3 | 41.2 | 44.1 | 47 |
| **Roll** | 37.8 | 39.7 | 41.5 | 43.3 | 45.2 | 47 | 48.8 | 50.6 | 52.5 |
| **In:out-roll** | 0.8 | 1.2 | 1.7 | 2.1 | 2.6 | 3 | 3.5 | 3.9 | 4.4 |

**Stats that we usually want to minimize** (i.e. SFB, SFS, Scissors, Redir and Pinky off) **can be referred to as negative. For these, we use a limited range for each stat.** If we did otherwise, the categories below would lose most of their usefulness. For example, although we could potentially make a layout with 20% SFB, there is never a need to make a layout with SFBs anywhere that high. The drawback with not being able to use the full range for these later stats is that the values chosen are intrinsically subjective. Regardless, most people should be satisfied when they see the results from using these ranges:

|  | Min | Very low | Low | Mid low | Mid | Mid high | High | Very high | Max |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **SFB** | 0.525 | 0.625 | 0.735 | 0.875 | 1.075 | 1.375 | – | – | – |
| **SFS** | 5.3 | 5.7 | 6.1 | 6.5 | 6.9 | 7.3 | – | – | – |
| **Scissors** | 0.1 | 0.15 | 0.25 | 0.35 | 0.45 | 0.55 | 0.7 | – | – |
| **Redir** | 2.8 | 3.6 | 4.5 | 5.4 | 6.2 | 7 | 9 | –  | –  |
| **Pinky off** | 1.8 | 2.7 | 3.5 | 4.3 | 5.2 | 5.9 | 6.8 | –  | –  |

Finally, hand balance is counted as **even** until a 52-48 split. Up to 55-45 it counts as **leans left/right**, and past that it counts as **heavy left/right**.

### 13.5. Hand balance nuances

As already explained earlier in this document, most layouts nowadays will place all the vowels on one hand. Doing this helps with minimizing long same hand sequences and redirects, in addition to improving rolling. The three main punctuation symbols will often go on the vowel hand as well, as vowels and punctuation usually share a column. Having the vowels plus punctuation together already adds up to around 40% usage on that hand.

A consequence of the above is that, **in layouts that dedicate a hand for the vowels, being strict with hand balance often results in too much finger movement being concentrated on the consonant hand**. For example:

| `w g d f v  j l u o , n s t h y  q r e a i ; b c m p k  z x / ' .` |
| :---- |

Another drawback with hand balance is that it can lead to the vowel side’s index finger being underutilized, while weaker fingers take that extra load. For instance, the above layout only has LR on the left index, yet it has a WNB pinky and a GSC ring.

In order to avoid the aforementioned issues, layouts that place all vowels on one hand will often be more lenient with hand balance and have a hand split of around 45-55 (e.g. Pine).  Other layouts go even further, like Sturdy, which has a 43-57 spilt:

| Pine (ClemenPine) `y l r m k  q f o u , c s n t g  b h a e i j x z w v  p d ' / .` | [Sturdy](https://o-x-e-y.github.io/layouts/sturdy/index.html) (Oxey) `v m l c p  x f o u j s t r d y  . n a e i  k q g w z  b h ' ; ,` |
| :---- | :---- |

# Chapter 14: Colemak-like layouts (4 min)

### 14.1. Colemak

Colemak is basically the “mainstream” alt layout. Technically, there is also Dvorak, but Dvorak has noticeably higher SFBs than modern layouts.

| [Colemak](https://colemak.com/) (Shai Coleman) `q w f p g  j l u y ; a r s t d  h n e i o ' z x c v b  k m , . /` |
| :---- |

**Colemak was designed around a few key principles**:

* Maximizing home row usage.  
* Concentrating effort on the indexes.  
* Minimizing pinky movement.  
* Favoring rolling.

|  | SFBs | SFSs | Scissors | Alt | Rolls | Redir | In:out-roll | Pinky off | Hand use |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **[Colemak](https://colemak.com/)** | **Mid high** 1.198 | **High** 7.462 | **Mid** 0.37 | **Low** 29.6 | **Mid high** 46 | **Very high** 12.1 | **Very low** 1 | **Min** 1.23 | **Hard right** 44 – 56 |

The main reason Colemak’s stats do not look very impressive is that Colemak was made in 2006\. Since then, keyboard layout analyzers have dramatically improved.

Additionally, the way some stats are defined has changed. For example, the **io** bigram used to always count as a roll on Colemak. However, nowadays there is more nuance to it. On the word **radio**, we indeed count **io** as a roll, but **io** often appears in the **ion** trigram, and that is a redirect on Colemak, not a roll. So, we can see how the redirect concept being introduced has led to Colemak receiving fewer rolls.

Similarly, the SFS concept did not exist back when Colemak was designed, which explains why the layout performs poorly in that aspect. Other concepts like SFBs, even if they did exist, have been optimized much further with the help of modern analyzers. In any case, **Colemak remains a very popular layout, even today.**

#### 14.2.2. FNHPB index \+ 4 vowels

The HNLM index in all the previous Colemak variants has the issue of concentrating a lot of movement (i.e. SFB \+ SFS distance) on that finger. **Here we use a FNHPB index instead, while the letter L is moved to a LR ring.** These changes have multiple advantages:

* Movement on the right index is greatly reduced.  
* The SFSs in the layout decrease by a lot.  
* Alternation, redirects and hand balance all improve a bit.

The following layouts differ from Colemak further. They aim to improve on Colemak’s SFBs, SFSs, rolls and redirects. However, some concessions have to be made in return. Namely, the pinky movement will increase.

| CSV ring \+ LRW middle | LR ring \+ CSG middle |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Isrt** (Whorf) `y c l m k  z f u , ' i s r t g  p n e a o  v w d j q  b h / . x` | **Irst** (Ec0) `y l c m k  z f u , ' i r s t w  b n e a o  j g d v q  p h " . x` |

|  | SFB | SFS | Scissors | Alt | Roll | Redir | In:out-roll | Pinky off | Hand use |
