Main **changes compared to Colemak**:

* the IY column is moved to the consonant hand, rather than A being there. Consequently, rolls increase while redirects decrease (the **YOU** and **ION** trigrams are not redirects anymore). The drawback is that Y is now on top row pinky.

* Punctuation no longer causes SFBs, as we have a ,A. ring (therefore avoiding Colemak’s **Y → period** 2U SFBs, and also the **E → comma** SFB).

* Movement on the right index is drastically reduced, thanks to using FNHPB over HNLM. It is recommended to put P next to H (see Irst) to improve **PH**.

* Different ring \+ middle setup. Isrt uses **CSV \+ LRW**. Although **LRW** is a high movement column, it allows us to get the letter L off the ring finger. Alternatively we can use **LR \+ CSG** (Irst) if we want to optimize SFSs instead.

# Chapter 15: Inward rotation layouts (18 min)

### 15.1. In-rolls & out-rolls

* **Inward rolls** go towards the index finger. E.g. Qwerty **DF** (middle  → index).  
* **Outward rolls** go towards the pinky. E.g. Qwerty **FD** (index → middle).

Some people prefer in-rolls over out-rolls, while others do not mind either way. One of the arguments often utilized in favor of in-rolls is that it is easier to smoothly roll our fingers on a table in the direction pinky → ring → middle → index, rather than the other way around.

**When optimizing for in-rolls we are restricted on which home rows we can use**. For example, a RSTH home row works great for in-rolls, but SHRT does not. **Similarly, we must also avoid using certain letter columns.** For instance, the popular NH column stops being an option. Not having certain columns available results in in-roll layouts having higher SFBs on average.

Additionally, **more letters are pushed toward the pinky corners when favoring in-rolls**. Because of this, it may be preferable to settle for arrangements that give up a bit of inward rotation, in order to avoid the pinkies being too heavy (e.g. a PNB pinky, E being on pinky…).

To sum up, there are multiple concessions that have to be made in order to design an inward rotation layout. Whether the in-rolls are worth those trade-offs or not is subjective.

### 15.2. How to arrange the vowels for in-rolls

#### YI OE UA vowel block

| [Hieamtsrn](https://mathematicalmulticore.wordpress.com/the-keyboard-layout-project/#comment-4976) (Sasha Viminitz) `b y o u '  k d c l p q h i e a ,  m t s r n v x ( ) . ?  w g f j z` |  |  |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |

The OE and UA columns must be placed on the middle and index fingers respectively, in order to make the **OU** bigram (on the top row) and the **EA** bigram (on the home row) both in-rolls. Furthermore, punctuation being on the index finger makes **E → comma/period** and **I/E → apostrophe** inward.

With this setup, the consonants on the vowel side (e.g. **H**) must go on pinky. Therefore, **this vowel arrangement is ideal for consonants that roll as consonant → vowel** since, by placing them on pinky, their bigrams will be inward (e.g. rolls like **HE**, **HA** or **HI**).

#### YI OA UE,  I OA UE  &  E OA UI vowel blocks

| [APT](https://github.com/Apsu/APT#aptv3-layout) (Eve) `w g d f b  q l u o y r s t h k  j n e a i ; X c m p v  z , . ' /` | Wreathy (Eve) `q g d f v  j l u o , n s t h y  w r e a i ; b c m p k  z x / ' .`  | Mir (RusDoomer) `j o u r q  f d l b g   e a i n x  y h t s c ' / . , z ;  k p m v w` |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |

On the vowel side, it is now the index finger that is free for consonants (e.g. **N** and **R**). So, **these vowel arrangements are ideal for consonants that roll as vowel → consonant** since, by placing them on index, their bigrams will be inward (eg. rolls like **IN**, **AN** or **EN**…).

Of the three vowel blocks right above, the third has the highest inward rotation as it is the only one where both the **OU** and **EA** bigrams are inward rolls. However, that vowel block requires placing E (the most frequently used letter in the English language) on a pinky.

### 15.3. How to arrange the consonants for in-rolls

As a whole, the consonants roll with the vowels in both directions about equally:

* **consonant → vowel** bigrams (e.g. NE) amount to **35.5%** of all bigrams.  
* **vowel → consonant** bigrams (e.g. EN) amount to **36.1%** of all bigrams.

However, **there are a few consonants that heavily favor one direction vs the other**. Those are the consonants we will be focusing on in-order to make inward rotation layouts.

#### 14.3.1. Consonants on the vowel hand

The table below shows the direction each consonant favors with the vowels (consonant → vowel vs vowel → consonant). The table is sorted based on the ratio, which is the result of dividing the first two columns (the higher number is divided by the smaller one):

|   `c→v` `v→c Favored direction` `ratio` `h` `5.322` `0.064 H → vowel` `83.2` `n` `1.921` `8.025 Vowel → N` `4.18` `w` `1.343` `0.508 W → vowel` `2.64` `b` `1.209` `0.541 B → vowel` `2.23` `s 2.409 4.083 Vowel → S 1.69` `p` `1.391` `0.824 P → vowel` `1.69` `k` `0.338` `0.233 K → vowel` `1.45` `v` `1.308` `0.929 V → vowel` `1.41` `y` `0.288` `0.402 Vowel → Y` `1.4`  |      `f 1.269 1.634 Vowel → F 1.29` `r 4.123 5.258 Vowel → R 1.28` `m` `2.127` `1.661 M → vowel` `1.28` `c` `2.428` `1.978 C → vowel` `1.23` `d` `1.746` `2.118 Vowel → D` `1.21` `g` `0.903` `0.801 G → vowel` `1.13` `t 4.374 3.87 T → vowel 1.13` `l 2.503 2.761 Vowel → L 1.10`  *\* table data: Norvig*  |
| :---- | :---- |

Among the highlighted top consonants, **H & N are by far the most one directional.** The letter H is better at minimizing out-rolls (it has a 83.2 ratio) while N can reach higher overall in-rolls (vowel → N is around 8% of all bigrams, while H  → vowel is around 5%). Since H and N roll in opposite directions, their ideal location is different. **On the vowel hand**:

* **H should go on the pinky** (to make **HE, HA, HI** and **HO** inward) **and we should pair it with the YI OE UA block** (as that vowel setup leaves the pinky free for H).

* **N should go on the index** (to make **IN, AN, ON** & **EN** inward) **and we should pair it with the YI OA UE, I OA UE** or **E OA UI blocks** (as they free the index for N).

#### 15.3.2. Consonants on the consonant hand

The table below shows the direction each consonant favors when combining with the rest of the consonants (consonant → rest vs rest → consonant). The table is sorted based on the fourth column (the ratio): 

|   `c→rest rest→c Favored direction ratio` `v 0.009 0.185 cons → V 20.6` `h 0.349 5.214 cons → H 14.9` `n` `4.764` `0.515 N → cons` `9.25` `y` `0.232` `1.501 cons → Y` `6.47` `d 0.445 1.868 cons → D 4.2` `b` `0.634` `0.166 B → cons` `3.82` `w` `0.558` `0.159 W → cons` `3.51` `k` `0.134` `0.33 cons → K` `2.46` `c` `1.639` `0.866 C → cons` `1.89`  |      `g 0.684 1.128 cons → G 1.65` `p 1.166 0.736 P → cons 1.58` `f` `0.525` `0.341 F → cons` `1.54` `t` `4.982` `3.638 T → cons` `1.37` `m` `0.61` `0.504 M → cons` `1.21` `r` `2.257` `1.933 R → cons` `1.17` `l 1.725 1.745 cons → L 1.01` `s 2.418 2.384 S → cons 1.01`  *\* table data: Norvig*  |
| :---- | :---- |

Yet again, among the top consonants, **H & N are the most one directional.** Interestingly, the direction each one favors has been flipped when compared to the previous table (e.g. before H rolled as H → vowel, but it now does as cons → H). Therefore, the preferred placements for H and N have been reversed. So, **on the consonant hand**:

* **H should go on the index**, to make **TH, CH, WH, SH** and **GH** inward.  
* **N should go on the pinky** (or ring), to make **ND, NT, NG, NS** and **NC** inward.

Other bigrams we want as inward if possible are: **ST, PR, CT, LY, LD, TR, RS, PL, MP, RY…**

#### 15.3.3. N & H on separate hands

**If we want the in-rolls in a layout to be evenly split across both hands, we should place N on one hand and H on the other**. Otherwise, the hand with both H and N will do a much better job at maximizing in-roll and minimizing out-rolls than the other hand.

### 15.4. Avoiding a NH column

**As we have established, N and H roll in opposite directions. This means that if we place them on the same finger, it becomes impossible to optimize in-rolls for both.** To visualize this, we will use a couple examples of layouts that disregard inward rotation:

| [Sturdy](https://o-x-e-y.github.io/layouts/sturdy/index.html) (Oxey) `v m l c p  x f o u j s t r d y  . n a e i z k q g w  b h ' ; ,` | Although Sturdy has lots of rolling there is not a net in-roll gain. This is because the in-rolls (all the vowel  → N bigrams) are offset by the out-rolls (all the H → vowel bigrams). |
| :---- | :---- |
| **[Stronk](https://o-x-e-y.github.io/layouts/stronk/index.html)** (Oxey) `f d l b v  j g o u , s t r n k  y m a e i z q x h p  w c ' ; .` | On Stronk the letter H leads to some key in-rolls (TH, SH) but the letter N causes some very common out-rolls (ND, NT, NS) |

If we want to maximize in-rolls, then H and N should be placed on different fingers, as such:

| Hyperroll (Semi) `p c l m v  x u o y f n s r t d  . a e i h b g ' w z  / , q j k` |  Hyperroll has the H → vowel bigrams as in-rolls, in addition to the N → consonant bigrams. |
| :---- | :---- |
| **[Vylet](https://github.com/MightyAcas/vylet)** (Acas) `w c m p b  x l o u j - r s t h f  y n a e i , q v g d k  z / ' ; .`  |  Vylet has the vowel  → N bigrams as in-rolls, plus the consonants → H bigrams.   |
| **Wreathy** (Eve) `q g d f v  j l u o , n s t h y  w r e a i ; b c m p k  z x / ' .` |  Wreathy has the N → consonant bigrams as in-rolls and the consonants → H bigrams too. |

As we can see, **inward rotation layouts should not use an NH column**. Note that, in layouts that disregard inward rotation, the NH column will be a very popular option.

### 15.5. In-roll ratio

**The in-roll ratio stat tells us how much a layout favors inward over outward rolls.** To calculate it, we simply divide a layout’s in-roll percent by its out-roll percent. For example, if a layout has 38.5% in-rolls and 14.1% out-rolls, then the in-roll ratio would be:

38.5 / 14.1 \= 2.7 in-rolls per out-roll

The **in:out-roll** column shows the in-roll ratio for a given layout:

|  | SFB | SFS | Scissors | Alt | Roll | Redir | In:out-roll | Pinky off | Hand use |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Hyper roll** | **Mid** 0.966 | **Low** 5.783 | **Mid** 0.45 | **High** 39.3 | **Mid high** 45.3 | **Very low** 3 | **Max** 4.2 | **High** 6 | **Even** 49 – 51 |

The layouts with the most in-rolls are those that have high overall rolls, while also maintaining a good in-roll ratio. For example:

### 15.6. Out-rolls vs alternation

Not all trigrams in a layout can be in-rolls. In fact, a significant part of trigrams will have to be either out-rolls or alternates. Depending on which of those two we favor, we will get a different type of in-roll layout:

* **If we want to minimize out-rolls, we must replace them with alternation**. This results in alternation heavy layouts, which have the highest in-roll ratio (**Hyperoll**).  
    
* **If we want to reach higher rolling, then some of the rolls have to be out-rolls**. Consequently, we get a rolling layout, but with a lower in-roll ratio (e.g. **Saiga**).

### 15.7. Layout arrangements for in-rolls

For more info on the layouts below, run them through the [Keysolve](https://grassfedreeve.github.io/keysolve-web/) web tool. That way you will get a nice heatmap of the layout, in addition to its lateral stretch and scissor stats. If you need help utilizing Keysolve, you can find it on the [Keysolve github page](https://github.com/grassfedreeve/keysolve-web).

**These layouts have H on the vowel hand and N on the consonant hand, both on pinky.** They are 1 vowel stack layouts (i.e. they have an **OE/OA column**, but not a NH/RH/RN one). Finally, they have high alternation and mid rolls.

# Chapter 16: High roll-mid redirect layouts (18 m)

### 16.1. Rolls & redirects

* **Roll**: pressing 2 keys with one hand, and 1 with the other (e.g. **DFJ** on Qwerty).  
* **Redirect**: a one-handed trigram in which the direction changes (e.g. **DFS** on Qwerty).

Generally, rolls are considered a comfortable hand pattern while redirects are seen as worse. So, **a desirable aspect would be having high rolls, yet low redirects.**

The issue is that increasing the former will do the same to the later. Having said that, while a certain amount of redirects is unavoidable, we can greatly reduce them by designing the layout adequately. In this chapter we go over how to do that.

Interestingly, we will find that the home row arrangements needed for high roll/mid redirects are at odds with those necessary for in-rolls. Therefore, none of the layouts in this chapter will favor inward rotation. In fact, their in-roll ratio will usually be below 1\.

### 16.2. Basics

As explained on section 8.7, any layout that aims to minimize redirects should follow two simple rules:

* **Have all the vowels on the same hand.**  
* **Move the letter H to the vowel side as well.**

Other than reducing redirects, we also want to increase rolling. For that we need to **move a few other consonants to the vowel hand, as H alone will not give us enough rolling.**

With all the above in mind, here is an example of a high roll/mid redirect layout. We see a H \+ vowels setup, with some consonants added on top of H for extra rolling:

| [Sturdy](https://o-x-e-y.github.io/layouts/sturdy/index.html) (Oxey) `v m l c p  x f o u j s t r d y  . n a e i  k q g w z  b h ' ; ,` | The letter H being on the vowel hand’s index finger will inevitably turn all the H \+ vowel bigrams (HE, HA, HI, HO) into out-rolls. This is why high roll/mid redirect layouts will not favor inward rotation. |
| :---- | :---- |

The setups that perform best at high roll/mid redirects are **FHNB \+ vowels, FHMB \+ vowels and HML \+ vowels.** Another option is **HRL \+ vowels**, but this last setups has higher redirects than the previous ones because of the presence of the letter R on the vowel side.

As seen on Sturdy, the consonants on the vowel side will be placed on the index, as that is the only finger that has room for six letters. That leaves the middle, ring and pinky fingers of that same hand for the vowels.

Aside from the vowel hand setup, the other aspect that affects how many redirects there will be on a layout is the home row on the consonant side (e.g. STRD on Sturdy). Having said that, the consonant hand has a much lesser impact on redirects than the vowel hand does. Because of this, we will be able to arrange the consonant hand in multiple ways depending on our preference, without that having too much of an effect on the redirects.

### 16.3. Layout arrangements for high roll \- mid redirects

For more info on the layouts below, run them through the [Keysolve](https://grassfedreeve.github.io/keysolve-web/) web tool. That way you will get a nice heatmap of the layout, in addition to its lateral stretch and scissor stats. If you need help utilizing Keysolve, you can find it on the [Keysolve github page](https://github.com/grassfedreeve/keysolve-web).

#### 16.3.1. NH \+ vowels

**This is the most popular high roll/mid redirect setup**. Aside from performing solidly at rolls/redirects, these layouts use optimized letter columns and also have low scissors (uncomfortable bigrams that involve pressing a key on the top row followed by the bottom row, or vice versa). **Their one drawback is poor hand balance.**

##### CRST

These are double stack layouts (i.e. **OA/OE column** \+ **NH column**) with a C pinky. Having C on pinky allows for more traditional index finger arrangements. However, this is usually at the expense of higher pinky movement.

### 16.4. Space thumb optimization

**Which thumb is used for space can have a significant effect on the alternate, roll, onehand and redirect stats.** In the following sections we investigate why this is the case.

#### 16.4.1. Space trigrams

Here we look at trigrams that include space. In other words, **trigrams starting with space (e.g. `[ th]`), with space in the middle (e.g. `[e t]`), or ending with space (e.g. `[he ]`).**

The following table shows the top 30 space trigrams on [the MonkeyType quotes corpus](https://monkeytype.com/quotes/english.json). The number next to each trigram indicates its frequency in percent (e.g. **\[ th\]** amounts to 1.780% of all trigrams).

|  `1-10 [ th] 1.780 [he ] 1.028 [nd ] 0.690 [ to] 0.623 [ an] 0.617 [ yo] 0.579 [to ] 0.566 [ng ] 0.542 [re ] 0.464 [ of] 0.455`  |  `11-20 [at ] 0.454 [e t] 0.430% [o f] 0.429% [ a ] 0.421% [ou ] 0.405% [ in] 0.400% [is ] 0.390% [ I ] 0.389 [ be] 0.378 [er ] 0.377`  |  `21-30 [ed ] 0.363 [ wh] 0.318 [e a] 0.315 [ll ] 0.315 [in ] 0.314 [t t] 0.309 [ wa] 0.286 [ it] 0.284 [ve ] 0.283 [ ha] 0.282`  |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |

\* You can find the full list [here](https://drive.google.com/file/d/16di2XwEkDqunpURUgJiUob-3XUwY-H3N/view?usp=sharing) (it was based on MonkeyType, as of October 3rd 2022).

It should not be surprising that space trigrams are very frequent, as space is easily the most common character. In fact, **trigrams including space amount to about half of all trigrams** (55.6% on the MonkeyType quotes corpus to be exact).

For this reason, layout stats will be wildly different depending if we account for space or not. When sharing stats for keyboard layouts, we usually give the stats disregarding space. Otherwise, the stats would have to be given twice (for right vs left thumb space).

#### 16.4.2. How rolls and redirects involving space work

Rolls with or without space are fundamentally different. **A sequence that is a roll when disregarding space may not be a roll anymore one space is included.** Take APT:

| [APT](https://github.com/Apsu/APT#aptv3-layout) (Eve) `w g d f b  q l u o y r s t h k  j n e a i ; x c m p v  z , . ' /` |
| :---- |

Without accounting for space, **TH** is a roll. If we use right thumb space for analysis, **space → TH** would still be a roll (**space** with one hand, **TH** with the other). However, with the left thumb, **space → TH** would now be a redirect (**space → T** is outward, but **T → H** is inward).

The following are APT’s stats with each thumb, using the [a200 analyzer](https://github.com/Apsu/200-analyzer):

|  `Left thumb space`  `Rolls 53.51%` `Alternates` `23.31%` `Onehands` `2.94%` `Redirects 8.39%`  |  `Right thumb space` `Rolls 44.03%` `Alternates` `30.49%` `Onehands` `4.84%` `Redirects 8.79%`  |
| :---- | :---- |

Interestingly, on APT we are not able to get the redirects down regardless of the thumb. This is partly because the consonant thumb makes **space → TH** (by far the most common space trigram) a redirect. Meanwhile, the vowel thumb will usually lead to lots of space trigrams being alternates or redirects, regardless of the layout.

**The solution is moving the letter H to the vowel hand** (as we have done in all the earlier high roll/mid redirect layout examples). **Then we can use the consonant thumb for space, without space → TH being a redirect.**

Technically, by making **TH** into an outward roll it becomes possible to have T, H and space all on the same hand without **space → TH** being a redirect. For example, if T was on the index finger and H on the middle, **space → T→ H** would be a 3roll.

#### 16.4.3. Example of analyzing space trigrams in a layout

The layouts that have the biggest variance on the stats depending on which thumb is being used for space are NH \+ vowel layouts. For example:

| [Canary](https://github.com/Apsu/Canary#canary) (Eve) `w l y p k  z x o u ; c r s t b  f n e i a '  j v d g q  m h / , .` |
| :---- |

**Let's go through the top 30 trigrams that include space, and see how they would be typed on Canary depending if we use the consonant or the vowel thumb for space:**

|  `Left thumb space   1-15 16-30 [ th] roll [ in] roll [he ] roll [is ] roll [nd ] roll [ I ] alternate [ to] roll [ be] roll [ an] roll [er ] roll [ yo] roll [ed ] roll [to ] alternate [ wh] roll [ng ] roll [e a] alternate [re ] alternate [ll ] - [ of] roll [in ] roll [at ] roll [t t] redirect [e t] roll [ wa] roll [of ] roll [ it] alternate [ a ] alternate [ve ] alternate [ou ] roll [ ha] roll`  |  `Right thumb space   1-15 16-30 [ th] alternate [ in] redirect [he ] redirect [is ] alternate [nd ] alternate [ I ] redirect [ to] alternate [ be] alternate [ an] redirect [er ] alternate [ yo] alternate [ed ] alternate [to ] roll [ wh] alternate [ng ] alternate [e a] redirect [re ] roll [ll ] - [ of] redirect [in ] onehand [at ] alternate [t t] alternate [e t] roll [ wa] alternate [of ] onehand [ it] roll [ a ] redirect [ve ] roll [ou ] redirect [ ha] onehand`  |
| :---- | :---- |

We can see that the space thumb makes a way bigger difference than we could have imagined. With the consonant thumb we get mostly rolls. Meanwhile, rolls plummet with the vowel thumb. To confirm the results above, the following are Canary’s stats on [a200](https://github.com/Apsu/200-analyzer) (using all space trigrams for analysis, not just the top 30):

|  `Left thumb space`  `Rolls 58.17%` `Alternates` `20.79%` `Onehands` `2.74%` `Redirects` `5.34%`  |  `Right thumb space` `Rolls` `41.51%` `Alternates` `29.89%` `Onehands` `5.71%` `Redirects` `9.92%`  |
| :---- | :---- |

#### 16.4.4. a200 analyzer

As a rule of thumb (;p), using space on the consonant side leads to higher rolls. Regardless, if we want to check the thumb stats for a particular layout, we can use the [a200 analyzer](https://github.com/Apsu/200-analyzer).

#### 16.4.5. Hand balance and space

Most layouts have higher use on the vowel hand. This is because vowels plus punctuation already adds up to around 40% use, then adding a few consonants on top of that can easily make that hand’s use to be 55% or even higher.

If the vowel hand is going to have higher use, it stands to reason that using the consonant thumb for space would be beneficial for balance, while using the vowel thumb would only exacerbate the problem.

The [Canary](https://github.com/Apsu/Canary#canary) layout perfectly exemplifies this issue. Disregarding space, its hand split is 42-58%. The space key has around 18.5% use. So, to get the hand split with space we just add 9.25% use to the space hand, and subtract 9.25% from the other hand. Doing this, Canary would have a 33-67 split with right thumb space, and 51-49 with left thumb\!

#### 16.4.6. Keeping your current space thumb

Most people do not want to change the thumb they have always used for space. Imagine someone that already uses the right thumb for space. If they want to learn a layout and it so happens that the left thumb is the “ideal” for it, they are unlikely to change thumbs.

A workaround is choosing a layout that has the vowels opposite to our current space thumb. This way we would already be using the “ideal” thumb. Alternatively, you could mirror the layout (swap the vowel and consonant hands) to achieve that same effect.

Regardless, choosing a layout based on space is a rather unreasonable proposition. **So, if the thumb you have always used happens to be the “ideal” one for the layout you want to learn, that’s great. If not, this aspect of layout design is often ignored.**

# Chapter 17: 3roll layouts (1 min)

### 17.1. 3rolls

A 3roll consists of pressing 3 keys with the same hand, all in the same direction (e.g. Qwerty **SDF**). **To maximize 3rolls, we must split the vowels** (usually 3 on one hand, 2 on the other) **in order to make crucial trigrams like THE, ING, AND,** **HER** **or** **ION into 3rolls**.

### 17.2. Layout arrangements for 3rolls

##### SEHT / REHT / INTS

Here we have a double stack variant with a C index (Seht Drai), and two 1 vowel stack variants (Ints and Snorkle):

| [Seht Drai](https://github.com/samuelxyz/layouts#seht-drai) (Tanamr) `f u l v b  q g n o j s e h t k  ' d r a i .  ; m p w z  y c x / ,` | Snorkle (Untwo) `. a y c j  q d l u x i o n s b  p t h e r , ' f g v  k w m ; z` | [Ints](https://github.com/samuelxyz/layouts#ints) (Tanamr) `f o u m j  q g d p , h a e r x  v s t n i  ' / l w z  y c k b .` |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |

Most layouts have between 2 and 4 percent 3rolls, these layouts go all the way up to 10 percent. So, **if we count both 2rolls and 3rolls, this style of layout has the highest overall rolling. Conversely, they have the lowest alternation as well.**

| **Snorkle** | **Low** 0.641 | **Low** 5.709 | **Mid high** 0.50 | **Min** 23.7 | **High** 48.4 | **Max** 9.8 | **Very high** 9.7 | **Very low** 1.0 | **Low** 3.2 | **Even** 50 – 50 |
| **[Ints](https://github.com/samuelxyz/layouts#ints)** | **Mid low** 0.779 | **Low** 5.749 | **Low** 0.24 | **Min** 21.2 | **Max** 50.8 | **Very high** 6.8 | **Very high** 12.3 | **Mid low** 1.9 | **Mid** 5 | **Leans left** 53 – 47 |

Ints performs better at inward rolls than the in-roll ratio stat above would suggest. This is because Ints has lots of inward 3rolls (the in:out roll stat is based on 2rolls alone). Anyway, the following are the main inward 3rolls on Ints:

* Left hand:  **HER, FOR, OUR, OUL, HOU**  
* Right hand: **ING, IND, INT, INK, ITY, INS**

# Chapter 18: High alternation layouts (15 min)

### 18.1. Alternation

Alternation consists of pressing a key with one hand, then one with the opposite hand, then back to the first. The advantage of alternation is that it feels rhythmic and minimizes awkward long same hand sequences. The drawback is that rolls will be lower.

**To achieve high alternation we place all vowels on the same hand, in addition to pairing the vowels with only certain consonants.** The following table shows which vowel hand setups lead to rolls or alternation:

| High alternation | High rolling |
| :---- | :---- |
| **H \+ vowels C/D \+ vowels S \+ vowels T \+ vowels** | N \+ vowels R \+ vowels L \+ vowels |
|  |  |

Note that the above is an oversimplification. It is possible to reach high rolling while having the letter H on the vowel side. We would simply have to add certain letters on top of H (e.g. NH \+ vowels, HML \+ vowels, LRH \+ vowels…).

### 18.2. Layout arrangements for high alternation

For more info on the layouts below, run them through the [Keysolve](https://grassfedreeve.github.io/keysolve-web/) web tool. That way you will get a nice heatmap of the layout, in addition to its lateral stretch and scissor stats. If you need help utilizing Keysolve, you can find it on the [Keysolve github page](https://github.com/grassfedreeve/keysolve-web).

#### 18.2.1. H \+ vowels

This is the most popular high alternation setup. **H \+ vowel layouts are best at maximizing alternation while simultaneously minimizing redirects.** Most of them are 1 vowel stack layouts (i.e. **OA/OE column**).

#### 18.2.2. C \+ vowels

**Compared to the H \+ vowel family, C \+ vowel layouts are not as good as minimizing redirects, but can reach lower SFBs.** These layouts will use two stacks (i.e. **OA/OE column** \+ **HN/RN/HR column**) and a “C index”. This refers to an index finger that pairs the letter C with consonants like Y, W, G, P… Such layouts have the absolutely lowest SFBs. This setup gives us a lot of freedom to arrange the home row in many ways.

# Chapter 19: Keyboard column analysis

In this chapter we look at each consonant individually, analyzing which letters can be paired with it. Basically, this chapter will give us a better understanding on why keyboard layouts utilize the consonant columns seen in [chapter 11]().

### 19.1 Info given for each consonant

#### 19.1.1. Pairs

If we add the **CR** bigram (0.149%) and the **RC** bigram (0.121%) we get the RC pair (0.27%). **The utility of pairs is that they show the SFB percent resulting from having two letters on the same column** (i.e. on the same finger).

For each consonant, we will be listing its pairs (excluding its X, J, Q, Z and vowel pairs). Moreover, we will divide pairs into four categories, based on their SFB percent. For example, the following are the pairs for the letter H:

|  `Minimal sfb ` `h + v 0.000 h + d 0.008` `h + f 0.002 h + m 0.013` `h + k 0.003 h + l 0.014` `h + b 0.005 h + n 0.037`  |  `Low sfb`  `h + y` `0.051`  |  `Medium sfb ` `h + p 0.095` `h + r 0.1`  |  `High sfb ` `h + g 0.228` `h + s 0.33` `h + w 0.384` `h + c 0.599` `h + t 3.686`  |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |

As a general rule, the **pink** column would be the pairs to avoid. The **yellow** pairs are perfectly viable, but could be better. Finally, the **blue** and **green** column pairs are best.

**Letters that have lots of minimal SFB pairs (e.g. T, H, D, C) are particularly useful for making index finger columns.** This is because there are many more letter interactions on the indexes (as each index is assigned six letters, rather than three like the other fingers).

#### 19.1.2. SFB thresholds

The corpus utilized to make the above tables was [Norvig](https://norvig.com/mayzner.html). The **green** column includes pairs up to 0.040% SFB. The **blue** column is for pairs up to 0.070%, and the **yellow** column is up to 0.178%. Pairs over 0.178% appear in **pink**. The last threshold was chosen so that the SC pair (which is needed in many layouts) still makes the cut on Norvig, while pairs like BY or YO (which layouts avoid) do not.

#### 19.1.3. Columns

After listing the letter pairs and their SFB percent for a given consonant, we will then list its most relevant letter columns. Again, we will use the letter H as an example:

|  | Pinky | Ring  | Middle | Index |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **H** | FH(K|') | LH | HN(B|M|L) (D|L)HM HRL | With N: FNH(PB|M|PY|BKV) With D: FHDPBKVY can be combined freely as long as BY is avoided. FHDMK also works. With R: LRHK Other: FHPK(Y|BV|YV|Y '), LHM (K|KV) |

If you have read chapter 11, you should already be familiar with the above format. Regardless, it is explained below just in case.

**Table notes**

To represent letter columns we use the following format: HN(B|M|L). The letters outside the parentheses are locked. Then, we complete the column with one of the options from inside the parentheses. So, in this case we have three options: HNB, HNM and HNL. 

On the columns for the pinky, ring and middle fingers, the first letter given will be the top row character, then the home row, and lastly the bottom row (e.g. HNB has H on the top row). We will use the configuration that leads to the least movement. For instance, for a LRH index the table will show R on the home row, as placing H on the home row instead (i.e. LHR) would noticeably increase movement.

The suggested columns are adapted to that finger’s strength. For example, a high movement column like HNL can go on a middle finger, but not on a ring or pinky. Columns with low movement and no SFBs (e.g. FHK, FH') are a good fit for the pinky. Finally, columns for the ring finger would be somewhere in between (e.g. LHQ).

To help with readability, the letters X, J, Q and Z are omitted from the table. So, for example, when the table only specifies two letters (e.g. a LH ring) in a place where we are supposed to have three letters, it is because we must complete the column with X, J, Q or Z (e.g. LHQ). Same applies to, for example, a FNHPB index. That is five letters. So, we would complete that index column with one rare character.

#### 19.1.4. Distances

After listing the frequent columns for a given consonant, there will be tables showing the movement (SFB \+ SFS distance) for each column according to the [genkey](https://semilin.github.io/genkey/) analyzer and utilizing the MonkeyType \+ Typeracer corpus (Norvig only contains bigram data, not actual text, so it cannot be used for this purpose).

The numbers will be normalized, meaning the movement for each column has been divided by its usage. By doing this, it becomes apparent when a column optimizes movement poorly. For example, a LRW column is hardly optimal because, despite having significantly lower use than, for example, HNM, it has higher movement regardless.  
   
To indicate how much movement a column has we will use the following color code. From lower to higher: **green** → **yellow** → **orange** → **red** → **dark red**. Note that, depending on the finger, the same value will be given a different color. For example, a column with 0.4 movement will appear in green on the middle finger, as a strong finger like the middle can easily handle that. However, 0.4 would appear as orange on a ring, and as red on a pinky.

| H pinky columns `FHK Hyperroll` `0.07` `FH' Hrst` `0.11`  | H middle columns `HNB Semimak` `0.34` `DHM Pinball` `0.43` `LHM Seht Drai` `0.53` `HNL Uciea 0.67` `HNM Dhorf` `0.69` `HRL Flow` `0.69`  | H index columns (with N) `FNHPB Megamak` `0.6` `FNH  M Canary` `0.67` `FNH B     . Sturdy` `0.80` `FNHP     Y Snug` `0.88`  `NHPB  KV Stronk` `1.14`  `NH  MLK Colemak DH 1.44`  |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |

Like on the prior tables, the letters X, J, Q and Z are omitted to help with readability.

On the tables for the pinky, ring and middle fingers, the first letter on a column will indicate the top row character, then the home row, and lastly the bottom row (e.g. HNB has H on the top row). The tables for the indexes are structured differently. On these, the letters that appear on multiple rows of the table are kept on the same vertical line. For example, if you look closely, you will see that the letters on the left table are aligned like on the right:

| H index columns (with N) `FNHPB Megamak` `0.6` `FNH  M Canary` `0.67` `FNH B     . Sturdy` `0.80` `FNHP     Y Snug` `0.88`  `NHPB  KV Stronk` `1.14`  `NH  MLK Colemak DH 1.44`  |  `F` `N` `H` `P` `B`       `F` `N` `H`   `M`      `F` `N` `H`  `B`      `.` `F` `N` `H` `P`      `Y`   `N` `H` `P` `B`   `K` `V`    `N` `H`   `M` `L` `K`     |
| :---- | :---- |

This way we can easily compare which letters are shared (and which are not) between two indexes. For example, the indexes on Canary and Colemak DH share the letters H, N and M. However, they differ in that canary adds F on top of that, while Colemak adds L and K.

### 19.2. Movement on the index vs the other fingers

The three letters we place on the pinky, ring and middle fingers necessarily have to be one on top of another. However, on the index it becomes possible to move letters to the center column. Because of this, a column can have lower movement just by being on index. For example, take the LRW column in both of the layouts below:

| Isrt (Whorf) `y c l m k  z f u , ' i s r t g  p n e a o q v w d j  b h / . x` | Wreathy (Eve) `q g d f v  j l u o , n s t h y  w r e a i ; b c m p k  z x / ' .` |
| :---- | :---- |

On Isrt the letters L and W are far apart. By comparison, on Wreathy L and W are now closer to each other, meaning that the overall movement on that finger will be lower.

### 19.3. High movement columns and alt fingering

When we say that a column has high movement we are assuming that the keys on that column are being pressed only by its intended finger. In other words, potential alt fingerings are not being taken into account.

As explained in chapter 5, alt fingering refers to pressing a key with a finger other than the intended one in order to avoid a SFB. It usually consists of pressing an index finger key with the middle finger, followed by pressing a center column key with the index. For example, take this layout:

| Noctum (Oxey) `b g d l z  j f o u , n s t r k  y c a e i  v m h x q  p w ' ; .` |
| :---- |

The LRHK left index on Noctum has high movement as it concentrates multiple SFBs. However, this layout was designed so that the **RL, RK** and **LK** SFBs can be comfortably alt fingered. To type **RL**, we would press R with index and L with middle. For **RK** and **LK**, we would press R/L with middle, K with index.

So, as long as we do not mind alt fingering, having a high movement index is not necessarily an issue, as that can be solved by alt fingering some SFBs. On the contrary, If we do not like to alt finger and prefer typing everything normally, then we may want to avoid any high movement indexes. On fingers other than the index alt fingering becomes less viable, as such alt fingers are not very comfortable.

### 19.4. Index finger columns

#### 19.4.1. Standard fingering

Most index finger columns will have at least one rare character (i.e. X, J, Q, Z or if not that, at least K, V or apostrophe). There are two reasons for this.

Firstly, we do not want a single finger to have too much movement (i.e SFB \+ SFS distance). Naturally, index fingers have the most danger of this, as they have six keys assigned to them. Therefore, if some of the letters on an index finger already add up to enough movement, the remaining keys on that finger can be left for rare letters. An example is LRNXJQ. With L, R and N all on the same finger, we complete the column XJQ.

Another reason a layout may reserve a rare letter for each index finger is using it for the Qwerty B position (on the left index) and for Qwerty Y (on the right index) as those keys are the furthest from the index finger’s resting position. They are marked with an X below:

![][image176]  
So, for example, if we had a DTMGKJ column on one index, and a FNHPBZ on the other, Z and J would naturally go on the highlighted red spots:

| Isrt `y c l m k  z f u , ' i s r t g  p n e a o ; q v w d j  b h / . x` |
| :---- |

#### 19.4.2. Angle mod fingering

With angle mod we gain one comfortable left index key. We can see that there are now seven orange keys, while there used to be six. Again, Qwerty B/Y are marked with a red X:

![][image177]This additional index key is particularly useful in layouts that use the left index as a C index (i.e. an index that combines C with some of D, Y, M, W, F, G, P, B, V or apostrophe). Here are some examples:

| [Sturdy](https://o-x-e-y.github.io/layouts/sturdy/index.html) (Oxey) `v m l c p  x f o u j s t r d y  . n a e i  k q g w z  b h ' ; ,` | [Snug](https://github.com/mndscp/snug-keyboard-layout#snug-keyboard-layout) (Mainstream) `q l d m b  j f o u ' s r t c g  p n e i a  x k w v z  y h / , .` | Trendy (StronglyTyped) `k l h w '  z f o u j t r n d b  y s a e i  x m c p q  g v . ; ,` |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |

Layouts with left indexes like these are a better fit for angle mod. If we un-angle mod the layouts above, this is the result:

| [Sturdy](https://o-x-e-y.github.io/layouts/sturdy/index.html) (Oxey) `v m l c p  x f o u j s t r d y  . n a e i z k q g w  b h ' ; ,` | [Snug](https://github.com/mndscp/snug-keyboard-layout#snug-keyboard-layout) (Mainstream) `q l d m b  j f o u ' s r t c g  p n e i a z x k w v  y h / , .` | Trendy (StronglyTyped) `k l h w '  z f o u j t r n d b  y s a e i q x m c p  g v . ; ,` |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |

On sturdy, the letter W is now in a worse location than before, as it is now relegated to Qwerty B. Same applies to the letter V on Snug, or P on Trendy.

### 19.5. Main consonants

#### Letter T

The following are all the T pairs (excluding X, J, Q, Z and the vowels):

|  `Minimal sfb ` `t + v 0.001` `t + k 0.001` `t + d 0.004` `t + g 0.017` `t + b 0.02` `t + m 0.028`  |  `Low sfb`  `—`   |  `Medium sfb ` `t + f 0.087` `t + w 0.089` `t + p 0.11`  |  `High sfb ` `t + l 0.222` `t + y 0.244` `t + c 0.487` `t + r 0.787` `t + n 1.051` `t + s 1.391` `t + h 3.686`  |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |

The table below summarizes the main T columns:

| Pinky | Ring  | Middle | Index |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| (K|V)T | DT (B|M)TK | DT(K|B|M|G) MT(K|G) or LTM | DTM or DTPB, then some off K, V or G are added. W may be included as well. Sometimes, D goes with H or C instead. |

In most layouts T goes on the index finger as it makes for an index with high use yet low SFBs. Indexes with T can be divided into DTM or DTPB setups (ideally M and P/B should not share a finger, because of the MP and MB SFBs). If not on index, T often goes on the middle finger and is paired with two of D, M or K (e.g. DTM, DTK or MTK).

There are a few home rows that place T on the ring finger so that the common STR trigram is a 3roll, rather than becoming a redirect (e.g. home rows such as STRD or STRN). Rarely, T appears on pinky (e.g. KT, VT) as a high usage yet low movement column.

Note: Despite lowering SFBs, the GT pair noticeably increases SFSs (the verb get becomes a SFS, so does the common ght trigram, and inter-word skipgrams like going to…). So, if we want to avoid those SFSs, we should place G with S or on a C index, instead of with T.

| (B|P)N | PNB | HN(B|M|L) RN (may go on ring) LNM | Most N indexes use the NH pair. E.g. FNH(PB|M|PY|BKV) On in-roll layouts, NH is avoided. E.g. NPYF, RNB |

The HN pair is heavily utilized in layouts as it allows for columns that have high usage, yet low to moderate movement. A popular example is a FNHPB index (which can be modified to make other variants like FNHM or FNHPY). Aside from on index, NH is also common on the middle finger (e.g. HNB, HNM, HNL).

There are instances where the NH pair is avoided in favor of other alternatives:

* On the weaker fingers we use columns with a lower load. For example, on the pinky we can use BN or PN. On ring we can have both and make a PNB column.

* N may also appear on columns like a RN middle/ring or a LNM middle.

* On layouts that optimize for in-rolls it becomes necessary to split H from N. In-roll layouts that keep N on the consonant hand will often place it on pinky (to make bigrams like ND, NT, NG, NS and NC inward). Meanwhile, in-roll layouts that move N with the vowels will put it on the index instead (to make IN, AN, ON and EN inward).

| (V|F|B)S | FSV or BS(V|F) LS Some of the columns on the middle finger cell. | GS(V|F|W) YS(F|V) CS(V|G|W|F) | S indexes often have 5 of CSGVWYFB. The main potential SFBs when combining those letters are: YS, SC, BY, GS & WS. Ideally, we should avoid having S, C and Y all on the same finger, as that leads to the most SFBs. |

Many layouts utilize the SC pair despite it causing SFBs in some common words (e.g. school, screen or science). The reason is that the letter C can not go on the same finger as T, N, R or H (high SFBs). Therefore, if C is to share a column with one of the top consonants, the letter S is the only good option (e.g. a CSG middle, a CSGVW index, etc…).

By using two stacks (i.e. an OA/OE column plus a HN/HR/RN column) it becomes possible to decouple C from S. This allows for new possibilities like making a VS or FS pinky (commonly seen on minimal SFB layouts). Alternatively, we can make lower movement rings like FSV. For a bit more movement we could include G (e.g. GSV) or even Y (e.g. YSV). Additionally, the LS \+ RN consonant block also becomes a possibility. As for the letter C, it would now be paired with other moderately common consonants (e.g. D, W, G, Y…) rather than with S.

| FH(K|') | LH | HN(B|M|L) (D|L)HM HRL | With N: FNH(PB|M|PY|BKV) With D, FHDPBKVY can be combined freely as long as BY is avoided. FHDMK also works. With R: LRHK Other: FHPK(Y|BV|YV|Y '), LHM (K|KV) |

As mentioned earlier, the HN pair is very common in layouts (e.g. a FHNPB index). At the same time, there are other useful applications for H that only become possible once we split it from N. For instance, the letter D can not share a column with N (ND bigram) but it can with H. So, on the aforementioned FHNPB index, we could replace N with D, to make FHDPB. Other examples of letters that work better with H than with N are K, Y, L, F or V.

Because of the combination of H being a common letter plus also having lots of minimal SFB pairs, it fits perfectly on the index finger (similarly to T). Additionally, layouts that optimize in-rolls and have H on the consonant hand will place H on the index so that bigrams like TH, CH, WH, SH or GH are inward. On the middle finger H often goes with N (e.g. HNB, HNM). H almost never appears on the ring finger. H on pinky is mostly reserved for inward rotation layouts that turn all the H \+ vowel bigrams (HE, HA, HI, HO) into in-rolls.

Finally, unlike the other top consonants H does not cause SFBs with the apostrophe key.

| WR | (W|L)R | LR RN (may go on ring) LR(H|M|W) | R on index is rare as R lacks low SFB pairs. Some index examples are LRHK or RNB. |

R is the letter with the worst pairings. Firstly, it does not have a single minimal SFB pair. Secondly, its low SFB pairs are not great either, as they cause significant SFSs. The WR pair causes skip-1-grams on common words like were, work or world. Meanwhile, VR does the same on words like over, very, never or however. Consequently, R does not have any low movement pairs that are ideal for the pinky. Despite that, a WR pinky is required on inward rotation layouts that use the RSTH home row.

Overall, the most common place for R is on a LR ring, as that is ideal for minimizing SFBs. On the middle finger, other than RN, we could use HRL. Excluding HRL, none of the remaining combinations of L \+ R \+ another letter optimize movement very well. Having said that, some layouts use a LRW middle. LRM is even more rare.

Generally, on the index finger we want to have five or six decently common consonants, without that leading to high movement. Doing this with R is impossible, because of how few good pairs it has. Therefore, indexes with R tend to have just 3 or 4 common letters (e.g. LRHK, RNB…) while the rest of the index is completed with rare characters (e.g. X, J, Q, Z).

On modern layouts, the most common location for the letter L is on a LR ring. Since L and R are both problematic letters, by placing them on the same finger we gain a lot of freedom to design the rest of the layout. Furthermore, LR is very helpful for making low SFB layouts.

On the middle or index fingers, an LHM column is the option with the least movement. The one drawback of LHM is that it often leads to a heavier ring finger (e.g. a RN or DTK ring). If we want a lighter ring, we simply have to use a heavier middle/index finger setup (e.g. HNL, LNM, etc…).

Finally, there are virtually no layouts where L goes on the pinky.

|  `Minimal sfb ` `y + v 0.005` `y + w 0.006` `y + u 0.006` `y + k 0.006` `y + f 0.01` `y + g 0.029` `y + i 0.029` `y + p 0.037`  |  `Low sfb`  `y + h` `0.051` `y + c 0.055` `y + d 0.057`  |  `Medium sfb ` `y + m 0.086` `y + n 0.111` `y + s 0.154`  |  `High sfb ` `y + b 0.181` `y + o 0.186` `y + a  0.233` `y + e 0.236` `y + t 0.244` `y + r 0.256` `y + l 0.44`  |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |

Y usually goes on either a YI pinky, a C index or a H index. A few layouts pair Y with N, or even S, but that leads to noticeably higher SFBs. Despite the YU pair causing no SFBs, it is basically never used because it creates a very common Y\_U SFS in the word **you**.

#### Letter W

The following are all the W pairs (excluding X, J, Q and Z). Note that the vowel pairs are included, as W is a semivowel:

|  `Minimal sfb ` `w + v 0.000 w + f 0.002` `w + g 0.001 w + p 0.002` `w + c 0.001 w + k 0.003` `w + u 0.001 w + y 0.006` `w + b 0.001 w + d  0.012` `w + m 0.002 w + l 0.028`  |  `Low sfb`  `w + r` `0.044` `w + s` `0.059`  |  `Medium sfb ` `w + n 0.085` `w + t 0.089`  |  `High sfb ` `w + h 0.384` `w + i 0.375` `w + a 0.445` `w + e 0.478` `w + o 0.552`  |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |

The one way for W not to cause SFBs is to place it on either a C index or a C pinky. If the layout does not dedicate a finger to the letter C (because the SC pair is used instead) then W would go with R, S, N or T.

#### Letter M

The following are all the M pairs (excluding X, J, Q, Z and the vowels):

|  `Minimal sfb ` `m + v 0.000 m + h 0.013` `m + w 0.002 m + d 0.019` `m + k 0.002 m + l 0.028` `m + f 0.005 m + t 0.028` `m + c 0.007 m + n 0.037` `m + g 0.011`  |  `Low sfb`  `—`   |  `Medium sfb ` `m + y 0.086` `m + b 0.093` `m + s 0.158` `m + r 0.178`  |  `High sfb ` `m + p 0.255`  |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |

M is usually paired with T, N or H. It can also go on a C index, but that is more rare.

#### Letter F

The following are all the **F** pairs (excluding X, J, Q, Z and the vowels):

|  `Minimal sfb ` `f + v 0.000 f + w 0.002` `f + b 0.000 f + c 0.002` `f + y 0.001 f + h 0.002` `f + p 0.002 f + d 0.003` `f + k 0.002 f + m 0.005` `f + g 0.002 f + s 0.023`  |  `Low sfb`  `f + n` `0.068`  |  `Medium sfb ` `f + t 0.087` `f + l 0.118`  |  `High sfb ` `f + r 0.245`  |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |

F usually goes with either H or S. It could also go on a C index or a N index.

#### Letter P

The following are all the P pairs (excluding X, J, Q, Z and the vowels):

|  `Minimal sfb ` `p + v 0.000 p + w 0.002` `p + g 0.001 p + c 0.002` `p + k 0.002 p + d 0.003` `p + f 0.002 p + n 0.007` `p + b 0.002 p + y 0.037`  |  `Low sfb`  `—`   |  `Medium sfb ` `p + h 0.095` `p + t 0.11`  |  `High sfb ` `p + s 0.246` `p + m 0.255` `p + l 0.282` `p + r 0.516`  |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |

P causes the least SFBs either with N, or on a C index. Still, it may also appear with H or T.

#### Letter G

The following are all the G pairs (excluding X, J, Q, Z and the vowels):

|  `Minimal sfb ` `g + v 0.000 g + k 0.003` `g + w 0.001 g + m 0.011` `g + b 0.001 g + t 0.017` `g + p 0.001 g + y 0.029` `g + c 0.001 g + d 0.034` `g + f 0.002`  |  `Low sfb`  `g + s` `0.054 g + l 0.067`  |  `Medium sfb ` `— `  |  `High sfb ` `g + h 0.228` `g + r 0.297` `g + n 1.019`  |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |

G can with T, S or on a C index. The latter two options cause fewer SFSs.

#### Letter B

The following are all the B pairs (excluding X, J, Q, Z and the vowels):

|  `Minimal sfb ` `b + f 0.000 b + v 0.004` `b + g 0.001 b + d 0.005` `b + k 0.001 b + h 0.005` `b + w 0.001 b + n 0.006` `b + p 0.002 b + t 0.02` `b + c 0.003`  |  `Low sfb`  `b + s` `0.054`  |  `Medium sfb ` `b + m 0.093 b + r 0.138`  |  `High sfb ` `b + y 0.181` `b + l 0.24`  |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |

B can go with H, N, T or on a C index.

#### Letter V

The following are all the V pairs (excluding X, J, Q, Z and the vowels):

|  `Minimal sfb ` `v + w 0.000 v + c 0.000` `v + f 0.000 v + t 0.001` `v + g 0.000 v + s 0.002` `v + k 0.000 v + b 0.004` `v + h 0.000 v + y 0.005` `v + m 0.000 v + d 0.019` `v + p 0.000 v + l 0.035`  |  `Low sfb`  `v + n` `0.052` `v + r 0.07`  |  `Medium sfb ` `— `  |  `High sfb ` `—`    |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |

V goes best with H, T, S or on a C index.

#### Letter K

The following are all the K pairs (excluding X, J, Q, Z and the vowels):

|  `Minimal sfb ` `k + v 0.000 k + m 0.002` `k + b 0.001 k + g 0.003` `k + d 0.001 k + w 0.003` `k + t 0.001 k + h 0.003` `k + p 0.002 k + y 0.006` `k + f 0.002 k + l 0.03`  |  `Low sfb`  `—`    |  `Medium sfb ` `k + s 0.087` `k + r 0.1` `k + n 0.103` `k + c 0.118`  |  `High sfb ` `—`    |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |

K always goes with either T or H.
